questions.stem: A 72-year-old patient, with a history of cataract surgery and diabetes mellitus, presents with decreased vision one month after surgery. Examination reveals a honeycomb appearance or flower petal pattern of the retina. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old patient, with a history of cataract surgery and diabetes mellitus, presents with decreased vision one month after surgery. Examination reveals a honeycomb appearance or flower petal pattern of the retina. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: macular edema Explanation: The clinical scenario of 72 year old, h/o of cataract surgery, flower petal pattern of retina in examination leads to the diagnosis of CME (Cystoid macular edema) Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) Etiology: Ocular Treatment Complications: Post-surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, retinal detachment surgery), ocular laser therapy, and topical ocular medications. Retinal Vascular Disorders: Diabetic retinopathy, central and branch retinal vein occlusion, retinal telangiectasia, and hypertensive retinopathy. Intraocular Inflammations: Pars planitis, uveitis. Retinitis pigmentosa. Vitreomacular Traction: Associated with macular epiretinal membrane (ERM) and vitreomacular traction (VMT) syndrome. Systemic Diseases: Includes leukemia, chronic renal failure, and multiple myeloma. Miscellaneous Causes: niacin toxicity , PG analogues (risk factor for development of CME) Clinical Features: Visual Loss: Initial minimal to moderate vision loss, potentially leading to permanent vision decrease if persistent. Ophthalmoscopy: Reveals loss of foveal contour, retinal thickening, a yellow spot at the fovea, and a "honeycomb appearance" of the macula . Fluorescein Angiography: Shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames. {{caption_text}} Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Demonstrates loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening. {{caption_text}} Complications: Long-standing CME may result in a lamellar macular hole . Treatment: Addressing the Cause: Intravitreal anti-VEGF or photocoagulation for diabetic CME; discontinuing causative topical medications. Topical NSAIDs: Such as ketorolac, diclofenac, or profenac, are effective in preventing and treating CME. Topical/Systemic Steroids: Useful in established cases. Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): Oral acetazolamide may be beneficial, particularly in cases associated with retinitis pigmentosa. Central Serous Retinopathy (Option B) is characterized by "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns on FFA, and neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment on OCT. CSR typically does not present with the cystoid pattern seen in CME. Retinal detachment (Option C) Defined as the separation of the retinal pigment epithelium from neurosensory retina. Diabetic Retinopathy (Option D): Typically shows diffuse retinal thickening and other diabetic changes, not the cystoid spaces seen in CME. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
macular edema

Explanation:

The clinical scenario of 72 year old, h/o of cataract surgery, flower petal pattern of retina in examination leads to the diagnosis of CME (Cystoid macular edema)

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)

Etiology:

  • Ocular Treatment Complications: Post-surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, retinal detachment surgery), ocular laser therapy, and topical ocular medications.
  • Retinal Vascular Disorders: Diabetic retinopathy, central and branch retinal vein occlusion, retinal telangiectasia, and hypertensive retinopathy.
  • Intraocular Inflammations: Pars planitis, uveitis.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Vitreomacular Traction: Associated with macular epiretinal membrane (ERM) and vitreomacular traction (VMT) syndrome.
  • Systemic Diseases: Includes leukemia, chronic renal failure, and multiple myeloma.
  • Miscellaneous Causes:niacin toxicity , PG analogues (risk factor for development of CME)

Clinical Features:

  • Visual Loss: Initial minimal to moderate vision loss, potentially leading to permanent vision decrease if persistent.
  • Ophthalmoscopy: Reveals loss of foveal contour, retinal thickening, a yellow spot at the fovea, and a "honeycomb appearance" of the macula.
  • Fluorescein Angiography: Shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames.
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Demonstrates loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening.

 

Complications:

  • Long-standing CME may result in a lamellar macular hole.

Treatment:

  • Addressing the Cause: Intravitreal anti-VEGF or photocoagulation for diabetic CME; discontinuing causative topical medications.
  • Topical NSAIDs: Such as ketorolac, diclofenac, or profenac, are effective in preventing and treating CME.
  • Topical/Systemic Steroids: Useful in established cases.
  • Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): Oral acetazolamide may be beneficial, particularly in cases associated with retinitis pigmentosa.

Central Serous Retinopathy (Option B) is characterized by "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns on FFA, and neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment on OCT. CSR typically does not present with the cystoid pattern seen in CME.

Retinal detachment (Option C) Defined as the separation of the retinal pigment epithelium from neurosensory retina.

Diabetic Retinopathy (Option D): Typically shows diffuse retinal thickening and other diabetic changes, not the cystoid spaces seen in CME.

questions.stem: What is the preferred treatment for a benign tumour of the superficial parathyroid gland?
questions.stemHtml: What is the preferred treatment for a benign tumour of the superficial parathyroid gland?
questions.solution: on: The preferred treatment for a benign tumour of the superficial parathyroid gland is surgical resection, which involves removing the tumour to avoid complications. Since benign parathyroid tumours (often referred to as adenomas) can lead to conditions like hypercalcemia, surgery is usually the most effective and curative treatment. The main modality of treatment is as follows: Indications of parathyroidectomy: Severe symptoms Young age Markedly reduced bone density Serum calcium more than 11mg% Urinary calculi Neuromuscular symptoms Urinary calcium more than 400mg/24 hours Indications of surgery in an asymptomatic case are: Serum calcium 0.25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit of normal Bone mineral density (BMD) by DEXA; T score –2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third of radius Vertebral fracture Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day) or increased risk of stone formation by risk analysis Age <50 years When medical therapy is not possible Miami Protocol: An intraoperative PTH is measured If it has reduced by more than 50% than the preoperative value, it indicates surgical removal. Casanova test: It is to differentiate the recurrence site after Removal of all 4 Parathyroid gland and auto transplant of it. PTH measurements are taken from the neck vein & brachial vessel. A positive Casanova test is if 20 times higher concentration in the brachial vessel Contraindications of surgery: Absolute contraindication: familial hypercalciuric hypercalcemia Here, elevated calcium and PTH level but 24 hr urinary calcium and calcium to creatinine clearance are low. Parathyroidectomy does not cure hypercalcemia due to FHH syndrome. Relative contraindications: Controlateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Vocal cord dysfunction. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
on:
  • The preferred treatment for a benign tumour of the superficial parathyroid gland is surgical resection, which involves removing the tumour to avoid complications.
  • Since benign parathyroid tumours (often referred to as adenomas) can lead to conditions like hypercalcemia, surgery is usually the most effective and curative treatment.

The main modality of treatment is as follows:

Indications of parathyroidectomy:

  • Severe symptoms
  • Young age
  • Markedly reduced bone density
  • Serum calcium more than 11mg%
  • Urinary calculi
  • Neuromuscular symptoms
  • Urinary calcium more than 400mg/24 hours

Indications of surgery in an asymptomatic case are:

  • Serum calcium 0.25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit of normal
  • Bone mineral density (BMD) by DEXA; T score –2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third of radius
  • Vertebral fracture
  • Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day) or increased risk of stone formation by risk analysis
  • Age <50 years
  • When medical therapy is not possible

Miami Protocol:

  • An intraoperative PTH is measured
  • If it has reduced by more than 50% than the preoperative value, it indicates surgical removal.

Casanova test: It is to differentiate the recurrence site after Removal of all 4 Parathyroid gland and auto transplant of it. PTH measurements are taken from the neck vein & brachial vessel.

  • A positive Casanova test is if 20 times higher concentration in the brachial vessel

Contraindications of surgery:

  • Absolute contraindication: familial hypercalciuric hypercalcemia
    • Here, elevated calcium and PTH level but 24 hr urinary calcium and calcium to creatinine clearance are low.
    • Parathyroidectomy does not cure hypercalcemia due to FHH syndrome.
  • Relative contraindications:
    • Controlateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
    • Vocal cord dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents to the ER with complaints of epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, his heart rate is 120/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. There is tenderness, guarding, and rigidity on palpation. Based on the clinical presentation and the X-ray findings, what is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents to the ER with complaints of epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, his heart rate is 120/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. There is tenderness, guarding, and rigidity on palpation. Based on the clinical presentation and the X-ray findings, what is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.solution: ictid="d837e66d6a1692777202dc9564a29a">viscus perforation Explanation: The clinical presentation and the x-ray findings that show free air under the diaphragm, which is a classic sign of perforation, suggest hollow viscus perforation. A hollow viscus perforation occurs when there is a rupture or hole in a hollow organ (such as the stomach, small intestine, large intestine, or duodenum), allowing its contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. This leads to peritonitis, a potentially life-threatening condition. Clinical features: Acute onset of severe abdominal pain , often described as sharp or stabbing. Generalized peritonitis : Tenderness and guarding over the entire abdomen. Rigidity (board-like abdomen). Tachycardia is due to pain and a systemic response to infection. Hypotension due to septic shock or fluid loss into the peritoneum. Nausea and vomiting are common & fever may develop as a sign of infection. Causes: Peptic ulcer perforation (most common cause, especially in duodenum). Trauma (e.g., stab or gunshot wounds). Diverticulitis leads to colonic perforation. Inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., Crohn’s disease). Appendicitis that progresses to rupture. Foreign body ingestion leads to injury or perforation. X-ray findings: Free air under the diaphragm (classic sign) indicates that air has escaped into the peritoneal cavity. It may show air-fluid levels if associated with bowel obstruction. CECT: Most sensitive to detect minimal/suspected pneumoperitoneum. Management: Surgical intervention: Exploratory laparotomy done after stabilisation. Antibiotics : Broad-spectrum antibiotics are started to treat peritonitis and prevent septic shock. Fluid resuscitation : IV fluids are crucial to support blood pressure and organ function, especially in cases of sepsis. Incorrect Options: Acute cholecystitis (Option A) typically presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign, but it is less likely to present with generalised peritonitis (rigidity, guarding) or hypotension. Sigmoid volvulus (Option C) typically presents with abdominal distension and onstipation, may show a characteristic "coffee bean" sign on X-ray. {{caption_text}} Small bowel obstruction (Option D) can present with pain, distension, and vomiting, but the key finding in small bowel obstruction is dilated loops of bowel on X-ray, not free air (unless there is a perforation, which is less common). In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ictid="d837e66d6a1692777202dc9564a29a">viscus perforation

Explanation:

The clinical presentation and the x-ray findings that show free air under the diaphragm, which is a classic sign of perforation, suggest hollow viscus perforation.

A hollow viscus perforation occurs when there is a rupture or hole in a hollow organ (such as the stomach, small intestine, large intestine, or duodenum), allowing its contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. This leads to peritonitis, a potentially life-threatening condition.

  • Clinical features:
    • Acute onset of severe abdominal pain, often described as sharp or stabbing.
    • Generalized peritonitis:
      • Tenderness and guarding over the entire abdomen.
      • Rigidity (board-like abdomen).
    • Tachycardia is due to pain and a systemic response to infection.
    • Hypotension due to septic shock or fluid loss into the peritoneum.
    • Nausea and vomiting are common & fever may develop as a sign of infection.
  • Causes:
    • Peptic ulcer perforation (most common cause, especially in duodenum).
    • Trauma (e.g., stab or gunshot wounds).
    • Diverticulitis leads to colonic perforation.
    • Inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., Crohn’s disease).
    • Appendicitis that progresses to rupture.
    • Foreign body ingestion leads to injury or perforation.
  • X-ray findings:
    • Free air under the diaphragm (classic sign) indicates that air has escaped into the peritoneal cavity.
    • It may show air-fluid levels if associated with bowel obstruction.
  • CECT: Most sensitive to detect minimal/suspected pneumoperitoneum.
  • Management:
    • Surgical intervention: Exploratory laparotomy done after stabilisation.
    • Antibiotics: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are started to treat peritonitis and prevent septic shock.
    • Fluid resuscitation: IV fluids are crucial to support blood pressure and organ function, especially in cases of sepsis.

Incorrect Options:

Acute cholecystitis (Option A) typically presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign, but it is less likely to present with generalised peritonitis (rigidity, guarding) or hypotension.

Sigmoid volvulus (Option C) typically presents with abdominal distension and onstipation, may show a characteristic "coffee bean" sign on X-ray.

Small bowel obstruction (Option D) can present with pain, distension, and vomiting, but the key finding in small bowel obstruction is dilated loops of bowel on X-ray, not free air (unless there is a perforation, which is less common). In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals rigidity and guarding. Abdominal X-ray shows air under the diaphragm. The patient is taken up for surgery, and an ileal perforation is noted intraoperatively with gross contamination of the abdomen with enteric and purulent content. What is the appropriate management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals rigidity and guarding. Abdominal X-ray shows air under the diaphragm. The patient is taken up for surgery, and an ileal perforation is noted intraoperatively with gross contamination of the abdomen with enteric and purulent content. What is the appropriate management of this patient?
questions.solution: n> with enteric and purulent contents, faecal diversion via ileostomy is usually recommended. This helps to prevent further contamination and allows the infected peritoneum to heal while diverting the faecal contents away from the abdomen. Types of Stomas: Type Description Common Uses Reversibility End Colostomy Single opening from the proximal bowel. Often permanent. Used when the distal bowel is removed or left in place, e.g., Hartmann's procedure Often permanent Loop Ileostomy Loop of the bowel is brought to the surface, and an incision is made Temporary diversion, especially in emergencies, and easily reversible Usually temporary Double-barrel Colostomy Two stomas are created: one for faecal output and one for mucus discharge Rarely used; can be for cases requiring both resection and exteriorization, offering mucous fistula Can be temporary Permanent Ileostomy Terminal ileum is brought to the surface after a colectomy Used when reconnection is not planned, often after total proctocolectomy for conditions like FAP Permanent Incorrect Options: Resection and anastomosis (Option A) is typically used in cases of multiple perforations , malignancy , suspected gangrene , or if there is significant tissue loss. It is not recommended in cases with severe peritoneal contamination , as the risk of infection, abscess formation, and anastomotic leak is high. Primary repair (Option B) is typically reserved for small perforations with minimal contamination and no signs of peritonitis. Omental patch closure (Option D) : While duodenal perforations are often treated with an omentum patch without resection, ileal perforations with significant contamination generally require more aggressive management, such as an ileostomy, to prevent sepsis and further complications. @Neet_pg_bot

  • This is due to increased metabolism and excretion of folate

    • Megaloblastic anemia
    • Other folate deficiency complications

questions.stem: Which mutation is linked to the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.stemHtml: Which mutation is linked to the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.solution: Explanation: The Philadelphia Chromosome is a reciprocal translocation involving chromosomes 9 and 22 that is commonly identified in CML (chronic myeloid leukaemia). The two chromosome breaks lie within: ABL gene on chromosome 9 BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene on chromosome 22. Nonhomologous end-joining causes a reciprocal translocation , resulting in the formation of an oncogenic BCR-ABL fusion gene on the derivative chromosome 22, known as the Philadelphia chromosome. BCR-ABL fusion genes encode chimeric BCR-ABL proteins with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. Inversion (Option A): In an inversion, a segment of a chromosome is flipped within the same chromosome but remains in its original location. Example of inversion-related disorder: Hemophilia A (due to intrachromosomal inversion in the F8 gene). Deletion (Option B) involves the loss of a chromosome segment, leading to missing genetic material. Example of deletion-related disorder: Cri-du-chat syndrome (chromosome 5p deletion) Insertion (Option D) occurs when a segment of one chromosome is inserted into another chromosome without reciprocal exchange. Example of insertion-related disorder: Some cases of hereditary cancer syndromes due to gene insertions. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:
  • The Philadelphia Chromosome is a reciprocal translocation involving chromosomes 9 and 22 that is commonly identified in CML (chronic myeloid leukaemia).
  • The two chromosome breaks lie within:
    • ABL gene on chromosome 9
    • BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene on chromosome 22.
  • Nonhomologous end-joining causes a reciprocal translocation, resulting in the formation of an oncogenic BCR-ABL fusion gene on the derivative chromosome 22, known as the Philadelphia chromosome.
  • BCR-ABL fusion genes encode chimeric BCR-ABL proteins with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.

 

Inversion (Option A): In an inversion, a segment of a chromosome is flipped within the same chromosome but remains in its original location. Example of inversion-related disorder: Hemophilia A (due to intrachromosomal inversion in the F8 gene).

Deletion (Option B) involves the loss of a chromosome segment, leading to missing genetic material. Example of deletion-related disorder: Cri-du-chat syndrome (chromosome 5p deletion)

Insertion (Option D) occurs when a segment of one chromosome is inserted into another chromosome without reciprocal exchange. Example of insertion-related disorder: Some cases of hereditary cancer syndromes due to gene insertions.

questions.stem: A motorcyclist met with a road traffic accident and had a metacarpal fracture. Hypothenar atrophy is observed. Identify the nerve involved.
questions.stemHtml: A motorcyclist met with a road traffic accident and had a metacarpal fracture. Hypothenar atrophy is observed. Identify the nerve involved.
questions.solution: rong>Explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles. Any damage to the ulnar nerve in case of a metacarpal fracture can lead to hypothenar atrophy. Ulnar nerve supply in the hand: The ulnar nerve travels alongside the ulnar artery and gives off a palmar cutaneous branch before reaching the flexor retinaculum, supplying the ulnar side of the palm & enters Guyon’s canal & divides into: Superficial Branch: Supplies the skin of the medial 1½ fingers & Palmaris brevis. Deep Branch: Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand except muscles of thenar eminence & 1st two lumbricals and terminates supplying Adductor pollicis, aka Graveyard of Ulnar nerve. Guyon’s Canal (Ulnar Tunnel Syndrome): Compression of the ulnar nerve within Guyon’s canal at the wrist. Clinical Features: Claw-Hand Deformity: The ring and little fingers exhibit pronounced ulnar claw hand when compared to injury of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (ulnar paradox) due to preserved function of the FDP, resulting in marked flexion of DIP joints. Atrophy of the Hypothenar Eminence (Option B) Loss of Finger Abduction and Adduction Positive Froment’s Sign: Unable to hold the book between thumb and index indicates weakness in the adductor pollicis. DIP Of thumb compensates for adductor pollicis weakness and thumb flexion occurs. Radial nerve (Options A) Damage to the radial nerve leads to wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist) and loss of elbow extension. Musculocutaneous nerve (Options C) injury causes weakness in elbow flexion, forearm supination and shoulder flexion. Sensory loss on the lateral aspect of the forearm is also seen Median nerve (Options D) lesion causes difficulty flexing the index and middle fingers and loss of thumb opposition, but it does not affect hypothenar eminence. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
rong>Explanation:
  • The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles. Any damage to the ulnar nerve in case of a metacarpal fracture can lead to hypothenar atrophy.

 

Ulnar nerve supply in the hand:

The ulnar nerve travels alongside the ulnar artery and gives off a palmar cutaneous branch before reaching the flexor retinaculum, supplying the ulnar side of the palm & enters Guyon’s canal & divides into:

  • Superficial Branch: Supplies the skin of the medial 1½ fingers & Palmaris brevis.
  • Deep Branch: Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand except muscles of thenar eminence & 1st two lumbricals and terminates supplying Adductor pollicis, aka Graveyard of Ulnar nerve.

Guyon’s Canal (Ulnar Tunnel Syndrome):

  • Compression of the ulnar nerve within Guyon’s canal at the wrist.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Claw-Hand Deformity: The ring and little fingers exhibit pronounced ulnar claw hand when compared to injury of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (ulnar paradox) due to preserved function of the FDP, resulting in marked flexion of DIP joints.
    • Atrophy of the Hypothenar Eminence (Option B)
    • Loss of Finger Abduction and Adduction
    • Positive Froment’s Sign: Unable to hold the book between thumb and index indicates weakness in the adductor pollicis. DIP Of thumb compensates for adductor pollicis weakness and thumb flexion occurs.

 

Radial nerve (Options A) Damage to the radial nerve leads to wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist) and loss of elbow extension.

Musculocutaneous nerve (Options C) injury causes weakness in elbow flexion, forearm supination and shoulder flexion. Sensory loss on the lateral aspect of the forearm is also seen

Median nerve (Options D) lesion causes difficulty flexing the index and middle fingers and loss of thumb opposition, but it does not affect hypothenar eminence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with MEN-1 syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is associated with MEN-1 syndrome?
questions.solution: nown as Wermer syndrome , results from a mutation in the MEN-1 gene located on chromosome 11q13 . This gene mutation leads to uncontrolled mitosis in endocrine glands. The classic triad of MEN-1 includes parathyroid adenoma (the most common manifestation), pancreatic adenoma, and pituitary adenoma . Parathyroid involvement is typically the first and most frequent manifestation of this syndrome. Types of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia MEN Type I MEN Type II MEN Type III MEN Type IV Cause Defect of chromosome 11q13 causing MEN 1 gene mutation Also called Wermer’s syndrome Defect of chr.10 leading to mutation of RET gene Also called Sipple’s syndrome Also called MEN II B , it is a variant of Type 2 MEN Defect of chr.12 causing CDKN1B gene Tumors Included Parathyroid adenoma (most common) It presents with primary hyperparathyroidism (↑ PTH and ↑ Ca) All the 4 glands can be included. Rx: Total/subtotal parathyroid resection Parathyroid adenoma ( most common, and calcium can be normal) Medullary carcinoma thyroid ( most common) Parathyroid adenoma ( Presents as hypercalcemia) Pancreatic adenoma Presents as Gastrinoma or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome This leads to peptic ulcer disease in the duodenum, which is the leading cause of death in this type. Pheochromocytoma . Pheochromocytoma (Most important criterion for both MEN 2 and MEN 3): Presents with elevated blood pressure. Pituitary adenoma: Prolactinoma Pituitary adenoma: Prolactinoma, causing amenorrhea and Infertility Medullary thyroid carcinoma Calcitonin is the tumor marker present Cold nodules are seen on the thyroid scan Metastasis can be traced with PET scan Visible neck mass, causing dysphagia Rx - Prophylactic thyroidectomy Reproductive tract tumors Testicular tumors Neuroendocrine tumor (Cervix) Associated conditions Angioﬁbroma Collagenoma Adrenocortical tumor Carcinoid tumors/Argentaﬃnoma Pheochromocytoma (only in 1%) Congenital aganglionosis, Hirschsprung disease Marfanoid habitus Medullated corneal nerve ﬁbers Mucosal neuromas Megacolon and Multiple diverticulae Occasionally with Renal tumor Adrenal tumor Parotid tumor (Option B) : Parotid tumors are not part of the multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes. These tumors affect the salivary glands and are not associated with endocrine disorders. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) : While some renal manifestations may occur in MEN syndromes (such as in MEN IV), renal cell carcinoma is not a feature of MEN-1. It may be coincidentally present but is not a defining feature of the syndrome. Pheochromocytoma (Option D) : Pheochromocytoma is actually associated with MEN-II/Sipple syndrome & MEN-III, not MEN-1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic patient with alcoholic liver disease was given some anti-amoebic drugs. Later, the patient presented with nausea, vomiting, flushing and hypotension. What is the likely diagnosis
questions.stemHtml: A chronic alcoholic patient with alcoholic liver disease was given some anti-amoebic drugs. Later, the patient presented with nausea, vomiting, flushing and hypotension. What is the likely diagnosis
questions.solution: p> The patient's symptoms of nausea, vomiting, flushing, and hypotension after taking an anti-amoebic drug in the context of chronic alcohol use are indicative of a disulfiram-like reaction. Metronidazole is used in the treatment of amoebic colitis and liver abscesses, which has the potential to cause this reaction. Metronidazole has a structural similarity to disulfiram (the drug used to help people with alcohol dependence). Disulfiram works by irreversibly inhibiting ALDH , and metronidazole's action on ALDH mimics this effect, leading to the accumulation of acetaldehyde when alcohol is consumed. Delirium tremens (Option A) is a severe form of alcohol withdrawal that occurs typically 48-72 hours after the last drink in an alcoholic patient. Symptoms include confusion , hallucinations , severe agitation , and autonomic instability; it can also lead to cardiac arrhythmia. Alcohol withdrawal (Option B) occurs when a chronic alcoholic stops drinking, typically presenting with symptoms like tremors , anxiety , insomnia , nausea , sweating , and potentially seizures. However, the presence of flushing and hypotension after taking a drug strongly points toward a disulfiram-like reaction in the given condition. Hallucinosis (Option D) is a condition where the patient experiences visual or auditory hallucinations in the setting of acute intoxication or alcohol withdrawal, in the case of alcoholics. The patient's symptoms here are more consistent with a reaction from drug-alcohol interaction rather than hallucinations. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A patient has a fever, rash, and eschar formation due to a mite bite. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: ass="customMeta" data-dictid="ff3e9793d01692777182b598b4a090">bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi and is transmitted through the bite of an infected mite (specifically the chigger mite). The hallmark features of scrub typhus include fever , rash , and eschar formation at the site of the mite bite. The eschar is a necrotic ulcer with a characteristic black center, often seen in patients with scrub typhus. Rash involving the palms and soles are typically seen in the following diseases: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) Hand-foot-mouth disease (CoxSackie A virus) Secondary syphilis Scrub typhus Causative agent Orientia tsutsugamushi - It differs from Rickettsia both genetically and by its cell wall composition i.e. it lacks lipopolysaccharide layer . Vector Chiggers (larvae of trombiculid mite) Pathophysiology Scrub typhus is so named because it occurs in scrub vegetation i.e. low-lying trees and bushes. The bite of infected trombiculid mites transmits it. Among all stages of mite, the larvae (called chiggers) are the only stage that feed on humans . Hence, scrub typhus is also called chiggerosis . Mites can maintain the organisms through transovarial transmission . Orientia tsutsugamushi infects mononuclear cells but still produces fever and rash. Clinical features The classic presentation of scrub typhus consists of triad of an eschar (at the site of bite), regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash sparing palms and soles. Non-specific manifestations may appear early such as fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Complications such as encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia may occur rarely in the late stage (due to vascular injury). Investigations The Weil-Felix test shows OX K+ only. Treatment Doxycycline is the drug choice. Azithromycin is given alternatively and the drug of choice in children and pregnant women . Anthrax (Option A) : Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis and typically presents with a papule that ulcerates, forming an eschar , but it does not typically present with a generalized rash or fever in the same way as scrub typhus. Anthrax is more common in individuals who handle animal products. African tick typhus (Option C) : This is caused by Rickettsia africae and transmitted by tick bites. It presents similarly to scrub typhus with fever and eschar, but scrub typhus is more common in regions like Asia, whereas African tick typhus is more common in sub-Saharan Africa. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) (Option D) : RMSF is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by tick bites. It typically presents with fever , rash , and eschar , but the rash in RMSF tends to start on the wrists and ankles and spreads centrally, unlike the rash seen in scrub typhus. It also doesn't commonly feature an eschar at the site of the tick bite. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
ul>
  • Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism, is characterized by autonomous aldosterone production from the adrenal glands. The condition leads to increased sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubules. It is characterized by Hypertension, Hypokalemia and Metabolic Alkalosis (leading to muscle cramps).
  • The pathophysiology involves excess aldosterone stimulating the ENaC channel, resulting in increased sodium and water reabsorption while promoting urinary loss of potassium and hydrogen ions.

    • Conn Syndrome / Primary Hyperaldosteronism

    Definition

    Primary hyperaldosteronism characterized by excessive aldosterone secretion from adrenal glands with suppressed plasma renin

    Epidemiology
    • Most common cause of secondary hypertension (6-20% of adult hypertensive patients)
    • Higher prevalence in resistant hypertension (up to 30%)
    • 2x more common in women

    Etiology
    • Aldosterone-producing adenoma (50-60%)
    • Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia
    • Aldosterone-producing adrenal carcinoma (1%)
    • Familial hyperaldosteronism (Types 1-3)

    Pathophysiology
    • ↑ Aldosterone → ↑ Na+ reabsorption → plasma volume expansion
    • ↑ K+ excretion → hypokalemia
    • Can lead to tissue inflammation and fibrosis in heart, kidneys, vasculature

    Clinical Features
    • Resistant hypertension
    • Muscle weakness/cramping
    • Fatigue
    • Headaches
    • Polydipsia/polyuria
    • NO edema (due to spontaneous natriuresis)

    Lab Findings
    • ↓ K+ (can be normal in up to 38%)
    • ↑ Na+
    • Metabolic alkalosis
    • ↑ Urinary K+ excretion (>30 mmol/day)
    • Suppressed plasma renin
    • ↑ Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR)

    Diagnostic Criteria
    • Initial screening: ARR >40
    • Confirmatory tests:
      • Salt loading test
      • Fludrocortisone suppression test
      • Captopril suppression test
    • Imaging: CT scan for adenoma
    • Adrenal venous sampling for lateralization

    Treatment
    • Adenoma: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy
    • Bilateral hyperplasia: Medical management
    • Medical options:
      • Spironolactone (first-line)
      • Eplerenone
      • Amiloride

    Prognosis
    • Surgery: 30-60% cure rate for adenomas
    • High morbidity/mortality if untreated
    • May need long-term BP monitoring

    High-Yield Associations
    • Normal K+ doesn't exclude diagnosis
    • No edema despite hyperaldosteronism
    • Screen all resistant hypertension cases

    Metabolic alkalosis (Option A) is a characteristic feature of Conn's syndrome. This occurs due to increased urinary loss of hydrogen ions and bicarbonate retention, leading to alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis is actually one of the hallmark features of this condition.

    Hypertension (Option C) is a primary manifestation of Conn's syndrome. This develops due to increased sodium and water reabsorption leading to volume expansion. The increased blood volume and sodium retention directly contribute to elevated blood pressure.

    Muscle cramps (Option D) are commonly seen in patients with Conn's syndrome. These occur due to hypokalemia. The low potassium levels affect muscle function and can lead to weakness, fatigue, and cramping.

questions.stem: What type of sanitation facilities should be provided for the soldiers returning from war?
questions.stemHtml: What type of sanitation facilities should be provided for the soldiers returning from war?
questions.solution: g>Explanation: Trench latrine facilities serve as vital sanitation solutions, particularly in military environments. These setups involve excavating elongated trenches in the ground, fortified with materials to prevent cave-ins, and equipped with seating or similar structures for soldier utilization. They offer a straightforward and efficient means of waste disposal, particularly suited for temporary or field conditions. Key features of a basic trench latrine include: Trench dimensions typically measure 30 cm in width, with depths ranging from 90 to 150 cm, and lengths spanning 3 to 3.5 meters. Such specifications are designed to accommodate approximately 100 individuals efficiently. To uphold privacy and comfort, separate trench latrines are designated for male and female soldiers. Users are instructed to cover their waste with soil after each use, ensuring the maintenance of hygiene and sanitation standards within the facility. Incorrect Options: Pit method (Option A): The pit method involves digging a hole or pit in the ground for waste disposal. While similar to trench latrines, pit latrines typically have deeper holes and may not be as suitable for military settings due to the need for frequent relocation and potential health hazards. Dumping method (Option B): The dumping method typically refers to the disposal of waste in designated areas, such as waste disposal sites or landfills. This method may not be appropriate for soldiers returning from war, as it lacks privacy and sanitation measures. Acqua privy (Option D): An acqua privy is a type of water-based toilet system that uses water to flush waste away. While common in civilian settings, acqua privies may not be practical or feasible for military deployments, especially in remote or austere environments. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Trench latrine facilities serve as vital sanitation solutions, particularly in military environments.
  • These setups involve excavating elongated trenches in the ground, fortified with materials to prevent cave-ins, and equipped with seating or similar structures for soldier utilization. They offer a straightforward and efficient means of waste disposal, particularly suited for temporary or field conditions.

Key features of a basic trench latrine include:

  • Trench dimensions typically measure 30 cm in width, with depths ranging from 90 to 150 cm, and lengths spanning 3 to 3.5 meters. Such specifications are designed to accommodate approximately 100 individuals efficiently.
  • To uphold privacy and comfort, separate trench latrines are designated for male and female soldiers.
  • Users are instructed to cover their waste with soil after each use, ensuring the maintenance of hygiene and sanitation standards within the facility.

Incorrect Options:

Pit method (Option A):

  • The pit method involves digging a hole or pit in the ground for waste disposal. While similar to trench latrines, pit latrines typically have deeper holes and may not be as suitable for military settings due to the need for frequent relocation and potential health hazards.

Dumping method (Option B):

  • The dumping method typically refers to the disposal of waste in designated areas, such as waste disposal sites or landfills. This method may not be appropriate for soldiers returning from war, as it lacks privacy and sanitation measures.

Acqua privy (Option D):

  • An acqua privy is a type of water-based toilet system that uses water to flush waste away. While common in civilian settings, acqua privies may not be practical or feasible for military deployments, especially in remote or austere environments.

questions.stem: An alcoholic male patient diagnosed with hollow viscus perforation is taken up for laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 2 cm perforation is seen in the duodenal region, as shown below. How can this patient be managed?
questions.stemHtml: An alcoholic male patient diagnosed with hollow viscus perforation is taken up for laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 2 cm perforation is seen in the duodenal region, as shown below. How can this patient be managed?
questions.solution: tion: In case of a duodenal perforation , omental pedicle repair is the preferred method of treatment. The omentum , a highly vascular tissue, is mobilised and placed over the perforation. This provides a biological seal and promotes healing while reducing the risk of infection or further leakage. Duodenal ulcer perforation: Common with anterior duodenal ulcers. Presents with an acute abdomen with sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain, rebound tenderness, and air under the diaphragm in the radiograph. Management: Non-surgical: Nil per-oral IV antibiotics and PPIs Surgical: Initial empirical antibiotic treatment. The perforation is approached by a small upper midline incision Perforations <1cm are closed primarily and buttressed with a well-vascularized omentum Larger perforations & with fibrotic edges: Modified Graham's Repair or Omental Patch Repair. The vascularized pedicle of the greater omentum is patched over the defect. Bleeding duodenal ulcer: A posterior duodenal ulcer is the one that usually bleeds. It is due to the involvement of the gastroduodenal artery . This leads to hematemesis, melena or both i.e., an upper GI bleed. Bleeding is commonly associated with intake of NSAIDs . Management: Endoscopic: Done to find the bleeding source and manage bleeds endoscopically. Injection , thermal coagulation, plasma argon coagulation, mechanical clips, and fibrin glue are the methods used. (with or without adrenaline injection). Angiographic management: If endoscopic management fails. Surgical management: Exposure to the ulcer and ligation of the duodenum are the principles here. Duodenotomy Ligation of the bleeding vessel with truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty @Neet_pg_bot

tion:

Duodenal ulcer perforation:

  • Common with anterior duodenal ulcers.
  • Presents with an acute abdomen with sudden-onset, severe epigastric pain, rebound tenderness, and air under the diaphragm in the radiograph.

Management:

  • Non-surgical:
    • Nil per-oral
    • IV antibiotics and PPIs
  • Surgical:
    • Initial empirical antibiotic treatment.
    • The perforation is approached by a small upper midline incision
  • Perforations <1cm are closed primarily and buttressed with a well-vascularized omentum
  • Larger perforations & with fibrotic edges: Modified Graham's Repair or Omental Patch Repair.
  • The vascularized pedicle of the greater omentum is patched over the defect.

Bleeding duodenal ulcer:

  • A posterior duodenal ulcer is the one that usually bleeds.
  • It is due to the involvement of the gastroduodenal artery.
  • This leads to hematemesis, melena or both i.e., an upper GI bleed.
  • Bleeding is commonly associated with intake of NSAIDs.

Management:

  • Endoscopic: Done to find the bleeding source and manage bleeds endoscopically. Injection, thermal coagulation, plasma argon coagulation, mechanical clips, and fibrin glue are the methods used. (with or without adrenaline injection).
  • Angiographic management: If endoscopic management fails.
  • Surgical management:
    • Exposure to the ulcer and ligation of the duodenum are the principles here.
    • Duodenotomy
    • Ligation of the bleeding vessel with truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty

questions.stem: A patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy, and abdominal pain. She also has a history of mood disorders and recurrent kidney stones. Which of the following investigations would not be useful in arriving at the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy, and abdominal pain. She also has a history of mood disorders and recurrent kidney stones. Which of the following investigations would not be useful in arriving at the diagnosis?
questions.solution: arteries Explanation: The patient’s symptoms, including polyuria , polydipsia , lethargy , abdominal pain , and a history of recurrent kidney stones , strongly suggest a diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism , which can result in hypercalcemia . The most likely cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a parathyroid adenoma. Angiography of renal arteries is typically used to evaluate the renal vasculature in cases of renal artery stenosis or other vascular abnormalities. However, it does not provide useful information for diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism, which is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. Incorrect Options: Nuclear sestamibi scan (Option A) is used to identify parathyroid adenomas . It is a key investigation in the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism , especially in localising the adenoma. USG neck (Option B) can also help in visualising parathyroid glands and is commonly used for parathyroid adenomas . Dual energy radiographic absorptiometry (DEXA) (Option C) is a test used to assess bone density and is often ordered to evaluate for osteoporosis , which is common in primary hyperparathyroidism due to bone resorption from elevated calcium. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the role of inhibin?
questions.stemHtml: What is the role of inhibin?
questions.solution: lanation: Inhibin from the granulosa cells inhibits FSH secretion. It is a hormone primarily produced by the ovaries (in females) and testes (in males). It regulates the reproductive system by inhibiting the secretion of FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) from the anterior pituitary gland. Inhibin suppresses the FSH Inhibin B: Before ovulation Inhibin A: After ovulation Stimulates the secretion of FSH (Option A): Inhibin does not stimulate FSH release; instead, it inhibits it. FSH is involved in the growth and maturation of reproductive cells, but inhibin reduces its secretion once the follicle or sperm production reaches sufficient levels. Inhibition of PRL (Option C) and Stimulation of PRL (Option D): Inhibin does not directly regulate prolactin (PRL), a hormone involved in milk production. PRL levels are primarily controlled by dopamine from the hypothalamus and other factors, not by inhibin. Therefore, inhibin neither inhibits nor stimulates PRL production. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Feature of angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and glossitis is seen in which vitamin deficiency?
questions.stemHtml: Feature of angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and glossitis is seen in which vitamin deficiency?
questions.solution: strong>Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency, characterized by the classic triad of angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and glossitis. This vitamin plays a crucial role in cellular energy metabolism and maintaining the integrity of mucocutaneous surfaces . The deficiency typically manifests with inflammation of the lips (cheilosis) , painful lesions at the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis) , and inflammation of the tongue (glossitis) Additional manifestations include seborrheic dermatitis along nasolabial folds and photophobia. Vitamin B2 Deficiency Riboflavin (B2) deficiency Cause Malnutrition Malabsorption Certain medications Phototherapy Clinical features: Cheilosis, glossitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, seborrheic dermatitis, anemia, photophobia. Diagnosis: Clinical response to supplementation, EGR (Erythrocyte Glutathione Reductase) activity test, low urinary riboflavin. Treatment: Oral riboflavin 3-10 mg/day, balanced diet including dairy products Niacin (Vitamin B3) (Option A) deficiency presents as pellagra, characterized by the 4 D's: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death if untreated. While it can affect the mucous membranes, the classic triad of oral manifestations is not its primary presentation. Cobalamin (Vitamin B12) (Option C) deficiency primarily presents with megaloblastic anemia and neurological manifestations, including subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Oral manifestations are not the predominant feature. Vitamin C (Option D) deficiency leads to scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and petechial hemorrhages. While it can affect oral mucosa, it does not cause the specific triad of angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and glossitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A child was diagnosed with Turner syndrome. Which of the following are features of Turner syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: A child was diagnosed with Turner syndrome. Which of the following are features of Turner syndrome?
questions.solution: strong> The image shows a webbed neck , which is a characteristic feature of Turner syndrome . Turner syndrome (45, XO) is a chromosomal disorder characterized by the absence of one X chromosome in females. Turner syndrome has multiple clinical manifestations that can be categorized using the SABLCOWN mnemonic: Clinical Features of Turner Syndrome (Mnemonic- SABCLOWN) S Short stature Short 4th metacarpal Sensorineural hearing loss A Amenorrhea (Primary) B Barr body absent C Cardiac abnormalities Cystic hygroma Cubitus valgus L Low posterior hairline Lymphedema of hands and feet Low thyroid (Hypothyroidism) O Ovaries streak-shaped/underdeveloped Rudimentary uterus W Webbed neck N Nipples are widely spaced on a shield-shaped chest Normal intelligence Normal height (Option B): Short stature is a cardinal feature of Turner syndrome. Growth failure typically becomes evident by age 3-5 years, and final adult height is significantly reduced without growth hormone therapy. Decreased carrying angle (Option C): Turner syndrome is characterized by an increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), not a decreased angle. This increased carrying angle is one of the characteristic skeletal manifestations of the condition. Gynecomastia (Option D): Gynecomastia is not a feature of Turner syndrome. Gynecomastia is associated with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Turner syndrome typically presents with widely spaced nipples on a shield-shaped chest. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is the next appropriate step in management after the failure of the McRobert maneuver in a case of shoulder dystocia?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the next appropriate step in management after the failure of the McRobert maneuver in a case of shoulder dystocia?
questions.solution: ong> Explanation: Shoulder dystocia occurs when shoulders fail to deliver with easy pulling within 60 seconds after delivery of the fetal head Suprapubic pressure (also known as Rubin's maneuver ) is applied if the McRoberts maneuver fails to deliver the shoulders Suprapubic pressure can release an impacted anterior shoulder Woods maneuver (Option A): This rotational maneuver is performed after failed suprapubic pressure, not immediately after McRoberts. The Woods maneuver involves rotating the posterior shoulder 180 degrees toward the fetal back and is considered a third-line intervention. Gaskin maneuver (Option B): Moving the mother to all-fours position is attempted after failure of anterior maneuvers. While effective, it requires time to reposition the mother and is not the immediate next step after McRoberts failure. Zavanelli maneuver (Option D): This is a last-resort emergency procedure involving cephalic replacement followed by cesarean delivery. It carries significant fetal and maternal morbidity and is only considered when all other maneuvers have failed. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

  • Shoulder dystocia occurs when shoulders fail to deliver with easy pulling within 60 seconds after delivery of the fetal head
  • Suprapubic pressure (also known as Rubin's maneuver) is applied if the McRoberts maneuver fails to deliver the shoulders
  • Suprapubic pressure can release an impacted anterior shoulder

 

Woods maneuver (Option A): This rotational maneuver is performed after failed suprapubic pressure, not immediately after McRoberts. The Woods maneuver involves rotating the posterior shoulder 180 degrees toward the fetal back and is considered a third-line intervention.

Gaskin maneuver (Option B): Moving the mother to all-fours position is attempted after failure of anterior maneuvers. While effective, it requires time to reposition the mother and is not the immediate next step after McRoberts failure.

Zavanelli maneuver (Option D): This is a last-resort emergency procedure involving cephalic replacement followed by cesarean delivery. It carries significant fetal and maternal morbidity and is only considered when all other maneuvers have failed.

questions.solution: p> The clinical presentation along with histopathology showing epithelial ducts compressed and distorted by surrounding stroma, is characteristic of an intracanalicular Fibroadenoma. It does not present as a well-defined, mobile, painless lump, making it an unlikely diagnosis here. questions.solutionHtml:
p>
  • The clinical presentation along with histopathology showing epithelial ducts compressed and distorted by surrounding stroma, is characteristic of an intracanalicular Fibroadenoma.

Fibroadenoma

Definition
  • Benign tumours arising from the proliferation of glandular tissue in the breast

Prevalence
  • Most common in women aged 15-25 years.

Aetiology
  • Believed to be influenced by hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years
  • Molecular alteration: Alterations in MED12 gene.

Clinical Presentation
  • Painless, firm, rubbery, and mobile lumps
  • Described as feeling like a "marble in the breast."

Histopathology

  • Well-defined borders due to a fibrous capsule, with proliferating stroma potentially compressing and distorting glandular components.
  • The epithelium may be of 2 patterns:
    • Pericanalicular Pattern: Surrounded by stroma
    • Intracanalicular Pattern: Compressed and distorted by it.

Mammogram

Popcorn calcification on mammogram

Diagnosis
  • Triple Assessment: Clinical examination, radiological imaging (ultrasound), tissue sampling (core-needle biopsy)
  • Ultrasound: Helps distinguish fibroadenomas from cysts
  • Core-Needle Biopsy: Provides definitive diagnosis

Treatment
  • Conservative Management: Watchful waiting, regular monitoring
  • Surgical Excision: For larger fibroadenomas, those causing symptoms, or uncertain diagnosis
  • Giant Fibroadenomas: Over 5 cm, may require excision through submammary incision

Prognosis
  • Benign, does not increase the risk of breast cancer
  • Growth can vary, influenced by hormonal changes
  • Recurrence is uncommon

Relationship to ANDI
  • Categorised according to ANDI as:
    • Normal: Small fibroadenomas (≤1 cm)
    • Disorder: Larger fibroadenomas (≤3 cm)
    • Disease: Giant fibroadenomas (>3 cm), multiple fibroadenomas

 

Acute mastitis (Option A) is a breast infection, common in lactating women, presenting with pain, redness, swelling, and fever. It is caused by a bacterial infection but is unlikely here due to the absence of pain and inflammation.

Ductal ectasia (Option C) is a benign condition in older women, causing nipple discharge, nipple retraction, and breast tenderness. It does not present as a well-defined, mobile, painless lump, making it an unlikely diagnosis here.

Sclerosing adenosis (Option D) is a benign breast condition causing firm, palpable lumps, often associated with pain and calcifications. It is not typically mobile or rubbery, making it a less likely diagnosis.

questions.stem: In solid organ transplantation, which of the following organs is associated with a higher incidence of rejection?
questions.stemHtml: In solid organ transplantation, which of the following organs is associated with a higher incidence of rejection?
questions.solution: Survival after lung transplantation continues to improve over time; however, the rates remain lower compared to other solid organ transplants. Around 50% of lung transplant recipients will face at least one episode of acute rejection within the first year . Furthermore, by five years post-transplant , roughly half of recipients will have developed chronic rejection . Incorrect Options: Kidney transplantation: (Option C) Graft rejection rate for kidney transplants is quite low after the first year. Specifically, with living-donor kidneys , the 1-year survival rate is 98% , and with deceased-donor kidneys , the 1-year survival rate is 93% . At 5 years, the graft survival rate for living-donor kidneys is 85%, and for deceased-donor kidneys, it is 75% . By 10 years, the survival rates drop to 65% for living-donor kidneys and 48% for deceased-donor kidneys, indicating a gradual decline due to chronic processes rather than acute rejection episodes. Liver transplantation (Option D): Chronic rejection occurs in about 13-17% of recipients Intestinal transplantation (Option B): Chronic rejection occurs in about 10% of recipients. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old HIV patient presents with persistent headaches, confusion, and a gradual onset of fever. A lumbar puncture is performed, revealing an elevated opening pressure and a cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows a positive india ink stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old HIV patient presents with persistent headaches, confusion, and a gradual onset of fever. A lumbar puncture is performed, revealing an elevated opening pressure and a cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows a positive india ink stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: sion, gradual onset of fever, and the findings from the lumbar puncture (elevated opening pressure and a positive India ink stain) strongly suggest cryptococcal meningitis , which is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans . Cryptococcus neoformans is a fungal pathogen that commonly causes meningitis in immunocompromised individuals , particularly those with HIV/AIDS . The hallmark of cryptococcal meningitis in a CSF analysis is the positive India ink stain , which reveals the characteristic encapsulated yeast cells. The elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture is also a typical finding in this infection. Cryptococcus Spp. Cryptococcus is a true yeast. Capsule Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis. Serotypes A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii Virulence factors Polysaccharide Capsule : The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread. Melanin Production : Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses. Enzyme Production : The fungus secretes several enzymes, including: Phospholipase : Aids in tissue invasion and damage. Urease : Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread. Risk of infection Immunocompromised States: HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk. Geographic Location: Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions Environmental Exposure: Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans. Management of cryptococcosis Microscopy India ink - Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans Culture Sabouraud Dextrose Agar , forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies. Niger seed agar and bird seed agar : Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme. The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci. {{caption_text}} Antigen detection tests Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test Treatment Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status. Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes. Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk. Bacterial meningitis (Option A) : Bacterial meningitis would usually show neutrophilic predominance in the CSF, along with a much more rapid onset of symptoms. It also typically does not result in a positive India ink stain, which is specific to fungal infections like cryptococcosis. Viral meningitis (Option B) : This would generally show lymphocytic predominance in the CSF and would not give a positive India ink stain. The clinical presentation of viral meningitis is often less severe than what is seen in this case. Tuberculous meningitis (Option D) : Tuberculous meningitis can cause a similar presentation with elevated opening pressure and CSF abnormalities , but it would not be detected by India ink staining. Additionally, it would show lymphocytic predominance and might require acid-fast bacilli staining or PCR for diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

The hallmark of cryptococcal meningitis in a CSF analysis is the positive India ink stain, which reveals the characteristic encapsulated yeast cells. The elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture is also a typical finding in this infection.

Cryptococcus Spp.

Cryptococcus is a true yeast.

Capsule

Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis.

Serotypes

A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans

B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii

Virulence factors
  • Polysaccharide Capsule: The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread.
  • Melanin Production: Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses.
  • Enzyme Production: The fungus secretes several enzymes, including:
    • Phospholipase: Aids in tissue invasion and damage.
    • Urease: Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread.

Risk of infection

Immunocompromised States:

  • HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk.

Geographic Location:

  • Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions

Environmental Exposure:

  • Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans.

 

Management of cryptococcosis

Microscopy

  • India ink- Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells
  • Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans

Culture
  • Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies.
  • Niger seed agar and bird seed agar: Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme.
  • The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci.

Antigen detection tests

Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test

Treatment

  • Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine
  • Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status.
  • Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes.
  • Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk.

Bacterial meningitis (Option A): Bacterial meningitis would usually show neutrophilic predominance in the CSF, along with a much more rapid onset of symptoms. It also typically does not result in a positive India ink stain, which is specific to fungal infections like cryptococcosis.

Viral meningitis (Option B): This would generally show lymphocytic predominance in the CSF and would not give a positive India ink stain. The clinical presentation of viral meningitis is often less severe than what is seen in this case.

Tuberculous meningitis (Option D): Tuberculous meningitis can cause a similar presentation with elevated opening pressure and CSF abnormalities, but it would not be detected by India ink staining. Additionally, it would show lymphocytic predominance and might require acid-fast bacilli staining or PCR for diagnosis.

TNM Staging of Carcinoma lip: T Stage Tis: Carcinoma in situ T1 : Tumor ≤2 cm and ≤5 mm depth of invasion T2 : Tumor ≤2 cm and >5 mm but ≤10 mm depth, OR Tumor >2 cm but ≤4 cm and ≤10 mm depth T3 : Tumor >4 cm OR any tumor >10 mm depth of invasion T4 : Invasion of adjacent structures N Stage: N0: No regional lymph node metastasis N1-N3 : Based on number, size, and laterality of involved nodes M Stage: M0: No distant metastasis M1: Distant metastasis Management of Carcinoma lip: Early Stage (T1-T2N0) Wide local excision with 1 cm margins Consider elective neck dissection for tumours>2 cm or >4 mm in depth Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+) Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status) Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer) Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings Reconstruction Options Wedge excision and primary closure (for small lesions) Local flaps: Abbe-Estlander, Karapandzic, nasolabial Regional flaps: Forehead, cervicofacial Free tissue transfer: Radial forearm free flap, anterolateral thigh flap Management of the Neck Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumours (>2 cm, >4 mm depth) Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck Radiotherapy Adjuvant: For positive margins, perineural invasion, multiple positive nodes Definitive: For patients unfit for surgery or refusing surgery Brachytherapy: Can be considered for select early-stage lesions Chemotherapy Not routinely used in early-stage disease It may be combined with radiotherapy in locally advanced cases Follow-up and Surveillance Regular follow-up visits: Every 1-3 months for the first year, then gradually decreasing frequency @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ion of the primary lesion with lip reconstruction is necessary for the treatment of primary cancer, and given the presence of a palpable lymph node (suggesting potential nodal metastasis), modified radical neck dissection (MRND) is indicated to address any possible regional nodal spread.

TNM Staging of Carcinoma lip:

T Stage

  • Tis: Carcinoma in situ
  • T1: Tumor ≤2 cm and ≤5 mm depth of invasion
  • T2: Tumor ≤2 cm and >5 mm but ≤10 mm depth, OR
    Tumor >2 cm but ≤4 cm and ≤10 mm depth
  • T3: Tumor >4 cm OR any tumor >10 mm depth of invasion
  • T4: Invasion of adjacent structures

N Stage:

  • N0: No regional lymph node metastasis
  • N1-N3: Based on number, size, and laterality of involved nodes

M Stage:

  • M0: No distant metastasis
  • M1: Distant metastasis

 

Management of Carcinoma lip:

Early Stage (T1-T2N0)
  • Wide local excision with 1 cm margins
  • Consider elective neck dissection for tumours>2 cm or >4 mm in depth
  • Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts

Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+)
  • Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins
  • Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status)
  • Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer)
  • Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings

Reconstruction Options
  • Wedge excision and primary closure (for small lesions)
  • Local flaps: Abbe-Estlander, Karapandzic, nasolabial
  • Regional flaps: Forehead, cervicofacial
  • Free tissue transfer: Radial forearm free flap, anterolateral thigh flap

Management of the Neck
  • Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumours (>2 cm, >4 mm depth)
  • Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes
  • Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck

Radiotherapy
  • Adjuvant: For positive margins, perineural invasion, multiple positive nodes
  • Definitive: For patients unfit for surgery or refusing surgery
  • Brachytherapy: Can be considered for select early-stage lesions

Chemotherapy
  • Not routinely used in early-stage disease

Types of Tonometry:

1. Indentation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP by how much a plunger indents the eye; softer eyes indent more than harder eyes.
  • Schiotz Tonometer:
    • Most widely used tonometer in the world.
    • Advantages: Inexpensive, simple, and reliable.
    • Disadvantages: Gives false readings in eyes with abnormal scleral rigidity (e.g., high myopes, post-surgery).

2. Applanation Tonometry:

  • Concept: Measures IOP based on the force needed to flatten the cornea's surface (Imbert-Fick Law: P = W/A).
  • Goldmann Tonometer (Option B):
    • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
    • Technique:
      • Cornea is anesthetized and stained with fluorescein.
      • Cornea and biprisms are illuminated with cobalt blue light.
      • The prism touches the cornea, and the inner edges of two semicircles are adjusted to just touch.
      • IOP is read by multiplying the dial reading by ten.

Variable force tonometers:

  • Goldmann applanation tonometer → Gold standard
  • Perkins tonometer (hand held version of goldmann)
  • Draeger tonometer (measures wide range of IOP)
    • Draeger tonometer is similar to Perkins
    • It has a different set of prisms
    • It operates with a motor
  • Pulsair (non-contact tonometer)
  • Airpuff (non-contact tonometer)
  • Grolman (non-contact tonometer)
  • Tonopen (based on both indentation and applanation) (Option D)
  • MacKay Marg (based on both indentation and applanation)
  • Rebound tonometer
  • Transpalpebral Tonometer

Fixed force tonometer:

  1. Maklakov tonometer
  2. Barraquer tonometer

Hertel’s exophthalmometer (Option A) is used to measure the degree of exophthalmos (protrusion of the eyeball) in conditions such as thyroid eye disease.

Gonioscope (Option B) is a specialized lens used to visualize the iridocorneal angle, which is important in assessing angle-closure glaucoma.

of normal bone with disorganized, vascular, spongy bone, resulting from excessive osteoclastic activity followed by increased osteoblastic activity. It presents with a distinctive "cotton wool" appearance on an X-ray of the skull.

 

Clinical Features of Paget’s disease:

Asymptomatic in most cases: Often discovered incidentally via X-rays or elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP).

Symptoms:

  • Persistent, dull aching pain, which worsens at night or in warmth.
  • Deformities:
    • Lower limb deformities: Tibia bows anteriorly, femur anterolaterally, resulting in a thickened, bent limb.
    • Skull involvement:
      • Enlargement may cause tight-fitting hats.
      • Skull base flattening (platybasia) - gives a shortened neck appearance.

X-ray Findings in Paget's Disease of Bone:

Flame shaped lucency of tibia

Disease Phase

X-ray Findings

Early (osteolytic) phase
  • Localised bone resorption often appears as "flame-shaped" lesions along the bone shaft. (Option C)
  • The skull may show osteoporosis circumscripta (well-defined areas of bone loss).

Later stages
  • Bone thickening and sclerosis with coarse trabecular patterns.
  • Stress fractures are visible as fine cracks on the convex surface of long bones.
  • Pathological fractures may be present.”

 

Looser zones : Looser zones, also known as pseudofractures, are characteristic of osteomalacia or rickets. These are incomplete fractures due to defective bone mineralisation.

Sunburst pattern : This is seen in osteosarcoma, where aggressive bone growth produces a characteristic spiculated appearance due to new bone formation.

Ground-glass appearance: This is typically associated with fibrous dysplasia, where bone appears hazy due to disorganised fibrous tissue replacing normal bone.

 

Osteosarcoma (Options A) presents with symptoms of persistent knee pain and swelling, with pain worsening at night and not relieved by NSAIDs. Biopsy shows pleomorphism, large hyperchromatic nuclei, and bizarre giant cells producing unmineralised osteoid

Osteochondroma (Options B) presents with hard mass over the right tibia, imaging showing a sessile growth, and a biopsy showing a cartilage cap

Ewing’s sarcoma (Options D) usually affects patients younger than 20 years of age and usually arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones

questions.solution: en scenario featuring inattention, aggression, excessive talking, poor academic performance, and difficulty sitting still suggests Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) , which is managed with methylphenidate. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Aetiology Genetic Factors: Runs in families, with parents or siblings more likely to have the condition (DAT1 gene and DRD4 gene). Neurochemical Factors: Linked to dopamine dysfunction and noradrenergic system. Neurophysiological Factors: EEG usually shows theta and beta waves in the frontal brain. Neuroanatomical Factors: Decreased activity in brain areas like the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and basal ganglia. Developmental Factors: Prenatal and perinatal factors, such as premature birth, maternal infections during pregnancy, and low birth weight, may increase the risk. Psychosocial Factors: Severe abuse, neglect, or maltreatment can worsen or mimic ADHD symptoms. Clinical features Hyperactivity: Restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, inappropriate running and climbing, excessive talking, interrupting others. Attention Deficit: Short attention span, distractibility, difficulty following instructions, forgetfulness, disorganisation, procrastination. Impulsivity: Acting without thinking, difficulty waiting for their turn, interrupting others, blurting out answers. Other: Emotional lability, explosiveness, irritability, memory and thinking defects, specific learning difficulties, speech and Hearing deficits. Diagnosis For an ADHD diagnosis to be confirmed , symptoms must be present in at least two different environments , such as both school and home. This ensures that the behaviour is not limited to one specific context and indicates a broader issue with attention and self-regulation. Treatment Pharmacotherapy Stimulant Medication: Methylphenidate (1st drug of choice) Amphetamine (2nd drug of choice) Modafinil ( not FDA-approved ) (Option B ruled out) Non-stimulant medication Atomoxetine Bupropion ( not FDA-approved for ADHD ) Psychosocial interventions Atenolol (Option C) is a beta-blocker which is used in the treatment of hypertension. It has no role in the management of ADHD. Amitriptyline (Option D) belongs to the class of tricyclic antidepressant drugs (TCA). It has no role in the management of ADHD. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
en scenario featuring inattention, aggression, excessive talking, poor academic performance, and difficulty sitting still suggests Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), which is managed with methylphenidate.

 

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

Aetiology

  • Genetic Factors: Runs in families, with parents or siblings more likely to have the condition (DAT1 gene and DRD4 gene).
  • Neurochemical Factors: Linked to dopamine dysfunction and noradrenergic system.
  • Neurophysiological Factors: EEG usually shows theta and beta waves in the frontal brain.
  • Neuroanatomical Factors: Decreased activity in brain areas like the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and basal ganglia.
  • Developmental Factors: Prenatal and perinatal factors, such as premature birth, maternal infections during pregnancy, and low birth weight, may increase the risk.
  • Psychosocial Factors: Severe abuse, neglect, or maltreatment can worsen or mimic ADHD symptoms.

Clinical features

  • Hyperactivity: Restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, inappropriate running and climbing, excessive talking, interrupting others.
  • Attention Deficit: Short attention span, distractibility, difficulty following instructions, forgetfulness, disorganisation, procrastination.
  • Impulsivity: Acting without thinking, difficulty waiting for their turn, interrupting others, blurting out answers.
  • Other: Emotional lability, explosiveness, irritability, memory and thinking defects, specific learning difficulties, speech and Hearing deficits.

Diagnosis

For an ADHD diagnosis to be confirmed, symptoms must be present in at least two different environments, such as both school and home. This ensures that the behaviour is not limited to one specific context and indicates a broader issue with attention and self-regulation.

Treatment

Pharmacotherapy

questions.stemHtml: A log dose-response curve (DRC) was plotted with isoprenaline alone and with isoprenaline in the presence of propranolol, as shown below. The graph shows that propranolol is a:
questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="90b63cdcfe16927771885e9612aecb">graph shows a parallel shift to the right, indicating that propranolol is a competitive antagonist of isoprenaline. Competitive antagonists work by reversibly binding to the same receptor as the agonist (in this case, isoprenaline ) but without activating the receptor. They compete with the agonist for binding sites. The agonist's maximum response can still be reached but at a higher dose of the agonist. In the presence of propranolol, the DRC for isoprenaline would shift to the right , indicating that higher concentrations of isoprenaline are required to achieve the same effect due to the competition for the receptor. Partial agonist (Option A) binds to the receptor and elicits a submaximal response , even when all receptors are occupied. This is not the behaviour described for propranolol, which is a beta-blocker and not a partial agonist. Agonist (Option B) activates a receptor to produce an effect similar to the physiological signal molecule. Propranolol is not an agonist because it does not activate the receptor. It is a beta-blocker and prevents isoprenaline from binding to and activating the beta receptors. Non-competitive antagonist (Option D) binds to a site on the receptor that is distinct from the agonist binding site and reduces the maximum response even if the agonist concentration is increased. In contrast, a competitive antagonist can be displaced by increasing the concentration of the agonist. @Neet_pg_bot
