questions.stem: Mid-year population is the denominator in?
questions.stemHtml: Mid-year population is the denominator in?
questions.solution: ion: The crude death rate (CDR) is a demographic indicator that measures the number of deaths in a population per 1,000 individuals per year. It is calculated by dividing the total number of deaths in a given period by the mid-year population and multiplying by 1,000. CDR = (Number of deaths / Mid-year population) x 1000 Therefore, the mid-year population serves as the denominator in calculating the crude death rate. This rate provides a broad overview of mortality within a population, irrespective of age or other factors. Incorrect Options: CFR (Option B): The case fatality rate (CFR) is a measure of the proportion of individuals diagnosed with a particular disease or condition who die from that disease or condition within a specified time period. It is calculated by dividing the number of deaths from the disease by the number of diagnosed cases and multiplying by 100 to get a percentage. CFR is commonly used in epidemiology and public health to assess the severity of a disease outbreak or epidemic. MMR (Option C): The maternal mortality rate (MMR) is a measure of the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. It reflects the risk associated with childbirth and pregnancy-related complications. MMR is an important indicator of maternal health and healthcare system performance, especially in developing countries where maternal mortality rates tend to be higher. NMR (Option D): The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) is a measure of the number of deaths among newborns (within the first 28 days of life) per 1,000 live births. It specifically focuses on mortality during the neonatal period, which is critical for assessing the quality of maternal and newborn healthcare services. NMR is an essential indicator for monitoring progress in reducing infant mortality and improving newborn health outcomes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A young male patient presents with sudden onset chest pain for one hour with ECG showing STE in lead 2,3 and aVF. Which is the best treatment for this case of inferior wall MI in a multispecialty hospital?
questions.stemHtml: A young male patient presents with sudden onset chest pain for one hour with ECG showing STE in lead 2,3 and aVF. Which is the best treatment for this case of inferior wall MI in a multispecialty hospital?
questions.solution: ifestations (sudden onset chest pain) with characteristic ECG findings (ST elevation in lead 2,3 and aVF) indicate an acute inferior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) . Primary angioplasty , also known as Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) , is the gold standard treatment for STEMI when performed at a capable facility within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Immediate Goals: Control cardiac discomfort. Rapidly identify patients for reperfusion therapy. Proper triage of lower-risk patients. Avoid inappropriate discharge of STEMI patients. Overall Aim: Initiate percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 120 minutes of first medical contact, including transfer to a PCI-capable facility if necessary. Alteplase (Option A): Alteplase, a tissue plasminogen activator, is only preferred in non-PCI-capable hospitals, where patients are further to be transferred to a PCI capable hospital. In a multispecialty hospital with PCI capabilities, primary angioplasty offers better outcomes with lower bleeding risk. Streptokinase (Option B): Streptokinase is no longer the treatment of choice according to current guidelines due to its risk of anaphylaxis and inferior outcomes compared to primary PCI. Dabigatran (Option D): Dabigatran is an anticoagulant and is not indicated for the treatment of STEMI. While anticoagulation is part of STEMI management, direct oral anticoagulants like dabigatran are not the primary treatment strategy in acute STEMI. PIM050 @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is the preferred drug for the treatment of postmenopausal breast cancer?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the preferred drug for the treatment of postmenopausal breast cancer?
questions.solution: Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor and is a standard treatment for postmenopausal breast cancer, particularly in hormone receptor-positive (HR-positive) breast cancer. It works by inhibiting the enzyme aromatase, which converts androgens to estrogens . Lower estrogen levels are effective in slowing or stopping the growth of estrogen-dependent breast cancer cells . Methotrexate (Option A) is a chemotherapy agent and immunosuppressant which is only used as part of a combination chemotherapy regimen including Cyclophosphamide and 5-Fluorouracil to treat early-stage breast cancer, especially where anthracyclines are contraindicated. Raloxifene (Option B) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) . It is FDA-approved for managing both the prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis . It is not considered the preferred treatment for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen (Option C) is also a SERM and is an effective treatment for pre-menopausal women. It works by blocking estrogen receptors on breast cancer cells, which can slow or stop the growth of tumors that require estrogen to grow. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
lass="customMeta" data-dictid="81d12f9cb01692777199e44ff3f3c1">surgical procedure performed to treat nasolacrimal duct obstruction, which causes epiphora due to impaired tear drainage. The surgery involves creating a new drainage pathway for tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity.

Indications for DCR:

  • Chronic dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac)
  • Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (either congenital or acquired, e.g., from trauma or aging)
  • Recurrent epiphora (despite conservative treatments)

Types of DCR:

  1. External DCR (Traditional):
    • Involves making an incision on the skin near the medial canthus of the eye .
    • The lacrimal bone (Mostly) and a portion of the maxillary bone are removed to create an opening between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity.
    • A stent is often placed to keep the passage open until healing is complete.
  2. Endoscopic DCR (Minimally invasive):
    • No external incision is made.
    • An endoscope is inserted through the nasal cavity to create a passage between the lacrimal sac and nasal cavity.
    • This approach is preferred for cosmetic reasons and for patients who may have anatomical difficulties with external incisions.

Postoperative Care:

  • Antibiotics are prescribed to prevent infection.
  • Stent removal (if placed) occurs after 6–8 weeks.
  • Nasal saline irrigation may be recommended to keep the new drainage pathway clear.

Complications:

  • Infection
  • Stenosis (narrowing) of the new drainage passage
  • Persistent epiphora or failure of the procedure

Serial beta hCG measurements are the first choice investigation for suspected ectopic pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive. Normal rise in early viable pregnancy shows doubling of beta-hCG levels over 48 hours Discriminatory zone (1500-2000 mIU/mL) represents the beta hCG level at which a gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound Abnormal rise or plateau suggests potential ectopic pregnancy and guides further management Diagnostic Modality Findings for Unruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Beta hCG Levels Failure to double the value of β-hCG in 48 hours Lower concentration of β-hCG than expected for gestational age Transvaginal Sonography (TVS) Absence of Intrauterine Pregnancy: No gestational sac within the uterine cavity when β-hCG ≥ 1500 IU/L. questions.solutionHtml:
">beta hCG levels

Explanation:

Serial serum beta hCG monitoring is the appropriate next step when transvaginal ultrasound is inconclusive in suspected tubal pregnancy.

  • Serial beta hCG measurements are the first choice investigation for suspected ectopic pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive.
  • Normal rise in early viable pregnancy shows doubling of beta-hCG levels over 48 hours
  • Discriminatory zone (1500-2000 mIU/mL) represents the beta hCG level at which a gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound
  • Abnormal rise or plateau suggests potential ectopic pregnancy and guides further management

Diagnostic Modality

Findings for Unruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

Beta hCG Levels
  • Failure to double the value of β-hCG in 48 hours
  • Lower concentration of β-hCG than expected for gestational age

Transvaginal Sonography (TVS)
  • Absence of Intrauterine Pregnancy: No gestational sac within the uterine cavity when β-hCG ≥ 1500 IU/L.
  • Adnexal Mass: An adnexal mass clearly separate from the ovary (Blob sign).
  • Ring-of-Fire Pattern: Increased blood flow around the ectopic mass on Color Doppler.
  • Presence of pseudo gestational sac.
  • Free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas

Transabdominal Sonography (TAS)
  • Absence of Intrauterine Pregnancy: No gestational sac when β-hCG ≥ 6,000 IU/L
  • Other features: May be visible but less sensitive than TVS for smaller masses

 

Methotrexate administration (Option B): Medical management with methotrexate is inappropriate without definitively diagnosing an ectopic pregnancy and ensuring specific selection criteria are met. Methotrexate is contraindicated if there is any possibility of a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

Laparotomy (Option C): Emergency laparotomy is reserved for patients with suspected ectopic pregnancy who are hemodynamically unstable or show signs of acute abdomen. This patient is stable and requires definitive diagnosis before any surgical intervention.

Diagnostic laparoscopy (Option D): While laparoscopy is the definitive diagnostic tool for ectopic pregnancy, it is too invasive as an initial diagnostic step when the patient is stable and diagnosis is unclear. Less invasive options like serial beta hCG monitoring should be exhausted first.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old obese female presented with Schizophrenia. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs causes the least weight gain?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old obese female presented with Schizophrenia. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs causes the least weight gain?
questions.solution: Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic that is known for having a relatively low risk of causing weight gain compared to other antipsychotics. It has a lower affinity for H1 histamine receptors (which are involved in appetite stimulation) and a high affinity for 5-HT2C receptors. Ziprasidone is often preferred in patients who are concerned about weight gain or who are already overweight or obese . Chlorpromazine (Option A) is a typical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 receptors to alleviate psychotic symptoms. It carries a risk for metabolic side effects like weight gain , diabetes , and hyperlipidemia . Clozapine (Option B) is an atypical antipsychotic that primarily works as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist , but it also has significant effects on serotonin receptors (5-HT2A and 5-HT2C). Weight gain is a common side effect of Clozapine . Olanzapine (Option C) is an atypical antipsychotic that is associated with weight gain and other metabolic side effects . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70 year old male patient presents to the OPD with multiple, recurrent fainting episodes. An ECG was taken and it shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and qrs complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 70 year old male patient presents to the OPD with multiple, recurrent fainting episodes. An ECG was taken and it shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and qrs complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: , characterized by complete heart block with recurrent syncope . The ECG findings show P waves at 75 bpm with QRS complexes at 35 bpm , demonstrating AV dissociation typical of complete heart block or IIIrd degree heart block . This indicates a complete interruption of electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles, leading to independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. Third-degree atrioventricular block / Stokes-Adams Syndrome Definition Complete failure of conduction between atria and ventricles, resulting in independent beating (AV dissociation). {{caption_text}} Ventricular Activity Maintained by an escape rhythm from: The AV node or bundle of His (narrow QRS complexes). Distal Purkinje tissues (broad QRS complexes). ECG Findings Prolonged PR interval Broad QRS complex Number of P waves will not be equal to the number of R waves P-R interval (atrial rate) will not match the R-R interval (ventricular rate) Clinical Features Recurrent syncope or 'Stokes–Adams' attacks- sudden loss of consciousness and collapse. Brief anoxic seizure. Pallor and a death-like appearance during the attack; characteristic flush upon recovery. Rapid recovery distinguishes it from epilepsy. Management Depends on clinical circumstances. Transient AV block in acute inferior myocardial infarction- no treatment if the patient remains stable. Symptomatic third-degree AV block- intravenous atropine or intravenous isoprenaline to maintain circulation until temporary pacing is inserted. Permanent pacemaker. Mobitz type II heart block (Option A) presents with intermittent failure of AV conduction with normal PR intervals 200ms. Unlike complete heart block, some P waves still conduct to the ventricles, and the pattern is not consistent with the current ECG findings. First degree heart block (Option C) shows prolonged PR interval >200ms with 1:1 AV conduction. This is typically asymptomatic and would not cause the presenting symptoms of recurrent syncope. Wolf parkinson white syndrome (Option D) presents with a short PR interval <120ms and delta waves. This represents pre-excitation through an accessory pathway and does not cause the AV dissociation seen in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

  • This indicates a complete interruption of electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles, leading to independent atrial and ventricular rhythms.

    • Third-degree atrioventricular block / Stokes-Adams Syndrome

    Definition

    Complete failure of conduction between atria and ventricles, resulting in independent beating (AV dissociation).

    Ventricular Activity

    Maintained by an escape rhythm from:

    • The AV node or bundle of His (narrow QRS complexes).
    • Distal Purkinje tissues (broad QRS complexes).

    ECG Findings
    • Prolonged PR interval
    • Broad QRS complex
    • Number of P waves will not be equal to the number of R waves
    • P-R interval (atrial rate) will not match the R-R interval (ventricular rate)

    Clinical Features
    • Recurrent syncope or 'Stokes–Adams' attacks- sudden loss of consciousness and collapse.
    • Brief anoxic seizure.
    • Pallor and a death-like appearance during the attack; characteristic flush upon recovery.
    • Rapid recovery distinguishes it from epilepsy.

    Management
    • Depends on clinical circumstances.
    • Transient AV block in acute inferior myocardial infarction- no treatment if the patient remains stable.
    • Symptomatic third-degree AV block- intravenous atropine or intravenous isoprenaline to maintain circulation until temporary pacing is inserted.
    • Permanent pacemaker.

     

    Mobitz type II heart block (Option A) presents with intermittent failure of AV conduction with normal PR intervals 200ms. Unlike complete heart block, some P waves still conduct to the ventricles, and the pattern is not consistent with the current ECG findings.

    First degree heart block (Option C) shows prolonged PR interval >200ms with 1:1 AV conduction. This is typically asymptomatic and would not cause the presenting symptoms of recurrent syncope.

    Wolf parkinson white syndrome (Option D) presents with a short PR interval <120ms and delta waves. This represents pre-excitation through an accessory pathway and does not cause the AV dissociation seen in this case.

questions.stem: A patient who received a supraclavicular brachial plexus block with 0.5% bupivacaine develops hypotension and arrhythmias. What is the first-line treatment for this situation?
questions.stemHtml: A patient who received a supraclavicular brachial plexus block with 0.5% bupivacaine develops hypotension and arrhythmias. What is the first-line treatment for this situation?
questions.solution: b83ec31581692777181547f1a89ef">Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) caused by bupivacaine as seen by the cardiac side effects (hypotension and arryhthmia). Treatment of choice is 20% intralipid infusion. Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): Clinical Features CNS effects: Early and less severe. First symptom: circumoral paraesthesia First sign: nystagmus At low plasma concentration: mild sensory disturbances. Increased concentration: CNS excitation, seizure activity. Higher concentration: CNS depression, coma, respiratory depression, arrest. Cardiac effects: Usually late but severe form of toxicity, may lead to death. Hypotension, dysrhythmias, myocardial depression. Potent agents (bupivacaine, ropivacaine, levobupivacaine) linked to cardiovascular collapse, heart block. Safety profile Bupivacaine has more risk to cause LAST than Lidocaine Most potent highly lipid soluble drugs are more likely to cause Prevention Risk recognition and dose reduction. Careful aspiration before injection. Incremental administration (3-5 mL) with continuous heart rate monitoring. Use ultrasonographic guidance to confirm anesthetic deposit. Use a vasoactive agent like epinephrine to reduce systemic absorption and serve as an intravascular indicator. Treatment Recognize LAST (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity) early and call for help. Airway management: Secure airway, ventilate with 100% oxygen. Administer 20% Lipid Emulsion: Bolus: 12 mL/kg over 2-3 min. Infusion: at 0.25 mL/kg/min-0.5ml/kg/min for 15-20 mins Maximum initial dose: 12 ml/kg Administration of antiepileptics: for seizure control, benzodiazepines such as Lorazepam is preferred. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: if necessary, monitor the patient at least for initial 2-6 hours following resuscitation. Since the question stem indicates hypotension and arrhythmia, this is not the correct answer. Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST):

Clinical Features

CNS effects:

  • Early and less severe.
  • First symptom: circumoral paraesthesia
  • First sign: nystagmus
  • At low plasma concentration: mild sensory disturbances.
  • Increased concentration: CNS excitation, seizure activity.
  • Higher concentration: CNS depression, coma, respiratory depression, arrest.

Cardiac effects:

  • Usually late but severe form of toxicity, may lead to death.
  • Hypotension, dysrhythmias, myocardial depression.
  • Potent agents (bupivacaine, ropivacaine, levobupivacaine) linked to cardiovascular collapse, heart block.

Safety profile

Bupivacaine has more risk to cause LAST than Lidocaine

Most potent highly lipid soluble drugs are more likely to cause

Prevention
  • Risk recognition and dose reduction.
  • Careful aspiration before injection.
  • Incremental administration (3-5 mL) with continuous heart rate monitoring.
  • Use ultrasonographic guidance to confirm anesthetic deposit.
  • Use a vasoactive agent like epinephrine to reduce systemic absorption and serve as an intravascular indicator.

Treatment
  • Recognize LAST (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity) early and call for help.
  • Airway management: Secure airway, ventilate with 100% oxygen.
  • Administer 20% Lipid Emulsion:
    • Bolus: 12 mL/kg over 2-3 min.
    • Infusion: at 0.25 mL/kg/min-0.5ml/kg/min for 15-20 mins
    • Maximum initial dose: 12 ml/kg
  • Administration of antiepileptics: for seizure control, benzodiazepines such as Lorazepam is preferred.
  • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: if necessary, monitor the patient at least for initial 2-6 hours following resuscitation.

Incorrect Options:

Invasive ventilation and Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (Option A and D): This is indicated only if there is a cardiac arrest. Since the question stem indicates hypotension and arrhythmia, this is not the correct answer.

Sodium bicarbonate can help correct metabolic acidosis, but it doesn’t target bupivacaine toxicity directly and is less effective in severe cases. Lipid emulsion therapy is considered the most effective treatment for life-threatening toxicity.

questions.solution: ng>primary hyperparathyroidism. The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary parathyroid adenoma . The characteristic findings of subperiosteal resorption on X-ray, along with elevated calcium and PTH levels and low phosphate , point towards this diagnosis. To localise the pathology (typically a parathyroid adenoma), the most appropriate imaging test is a 99Tc radiolabelled sestamibi scan . Sestamibi scan is a type of nuclear medicine-based study that is most accurate for parathyroid lesion localisation. It is safe and reproducible . It has a sensitivity and specificity similar to ultrasound but may detect glands in ectopic positions better. Sestamibi accumulates in the mitochondria, and henc,e the rates at which it washes out differ as per the number of mitochondria in different tissues. Parathyroid adenoma is rich in oxyphilic cells with a high concentration of mitochondria and, hence has a lower washout than the thyroid gland. False positives are rare, and the sensitivity and specificity are 79% and 90,% respectively. Addition of a thyroid specific radioactive tracer eliminates the chance of false positives. {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Other investigations: Parathyroid angiography and venous sampling for parathyroid hormone. Biochemical analysis is always to be done. Incorrect Options: Ultrasonography (Option C): Parathyroid adenoma is identified as an oval/ elongated, bi or multiloculated hypoechoic structure. Advantage: Can identify and facilitate biopsy of any concomitant thyroid pathology. Disadvantage : Adenomas in retro-oesophageal, retrosternal, or retro-tracheal areas can be missed. CT (Option D): Rapid uptake and washout allow hyperfunctioning glands to be differentiated from lymph nodes that demonstrate a progressive enhancement pattern. Disadvantage: Higher radiation dose than traditional imaging. Hence, it is not preferred. MRI (Option B): It is not commonly used, but it is helpful for preoperative cases or mediastinal adenomas. It has poor resolution for small glands/adenomas <5 mm, and it is difficult to localise superior glands. questions.solution: s of severe trauma , such as being run over or falling on railway tracks, injuries can be so extensive that amputation is necessary to prevent massive blood loss , gangrene , or infection , which can lead to death. The decision for a bilateral below-knee amputation is usually made as a life-saving measure when there is irreversible damage to the legs. Indications for Amputation: Dead Limb: Gangrene Deadly Limb Wet gangrene Spreading cellulitis Arteriovenous fistula Malignancy (e.g., sarcoma) Dead loss of limb: Severe rest pain due to irreversible critical leg ischemia Paralysis Severe contracture Trauma (irreparable damage) Local Amputation : For small-vessel disease (e.g., diabetes) : Gangrene of toes may require local amputation. Above-knee Amputation : For poor circulation or non-mobilizing patients. Knee Disarticulation : Preserves femur and patella for better prosthetic function. Post-operative care: Pain Management : Regular opiate use. Limb Care : Prevent pressure ulcers on the remaining limb. Exercise : Prevent deformities, build strength, and improve mobility. s of severe trauma, such as being run over or falling on railway tracks, injuries can be so extensive that amputation is necessary to prevent massive blood loss, gangrene, or infection, which can lead to death. The decision for a bilateral below-knee amputation is usually made as a life-saving measure when there is irreversible damage to the legs.

Indications for Amputation:

  • Dead Limb: Gangrene
  • Deadly Limb
    • Wet gangrene
    • Spreading cellulitis
    • Arteriovenous fistula
    • Malignancy (e.g., sarcoma)
  • Dead loss of limb:
    • Severe rest pain due to irreversible critical leg ischemia
    • Paralysis
    • Severe contracture
    • Trauma (irreparable damage)

Local Amputation:

  • For small-vessel disease (e.g., diabetes): Gangrene of toes may require local amputation. If the metatarsophalangeal joint is involved, ray excision may be necessary.

Major Amputation:

  • Below-knee Amputation: Preserves knee joint, offering better prosthetic use.
  • Above-knee Amputation: For poor circulation or non-mobilizing patients.
  • Knee Disarticulation: Preserves femur and patella for better prosthetic function.

Post-operative care:

  • Pain Management: Regular opiate use.
  • Limb Care: Prevent pressure ulcers on the remaining limb.
  • Exercise: Prevent deformities, build strength, and improve mobility.

Complications:

  • Early: Hemorrhage, infection, gas gangrene, and wound dehiscence.
  • Late: Phantom limb pain, stump ulceration, DVT, and pulmonary embolism

questions.stem: A 45-year-old alcoholic patient presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. Blood investigations reveal increased serum amylase and lipase levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old alcoholic patient presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. Blood investigations reveal increased serum amylase and lipase levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: pancreatitis Explanation: The patient's history of alcohol consumption, along with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and significantly elevated serum amylase and lipase levels , points strongly toward acute pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis: Clinical features: Pain ( severe , constant , and often resistant to common analgesics) . In about 50% of patients , the pain radiates to the back , and some patients may find relief by sitting or leaning forward . Nausea and vomiting are usually prominent, and retching may persist even with nasogastric aspiration. Examination findings: Patient's condition: well to severely ill with signs of shock and toxicity . Tachypnea , tachycardia , and hypotension are commonly observed. Mild icterus may suggest biliary obstruction (in gallstone pancreatitis). SIRS may be present Bluish discolouration ( Grey Turner’s sign or Cullen’s sign ). Abdominal distension due to ileus or ascites is common, and muscle guarding is often present. Diagnosis: Serum amylase level > 3x the normal value is strongly indicative. Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase. CECT scan is the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis. Management: Mild cases may be managed with IV fluids , analgesics , and antiemetics . Nil per os (NPO) is typically advised initially to avoid stimulating the pancreas. Antibiotics are not generally indicated unless there is suspicion of infection Management of severe cases: Admit to intensive care or a high-dependency unit for close monitoring. Aggressive fluid resuscitation is critical, guided by vital signs, urine output, and central venous pressure. Oxygen supplementation and serial blood gas analysis . If nutritional support is necessary, enteral feeding via nasogastric tube is preferred over parenteral nutrition. Management of specific complications: Antibiotics may be indicated if cholangitis or other infections are suspected. Prophylactic antibiotics should not exceed 14 days . If gallstone pancreatitis is suspected and there is biliary obstruction , ERCP should be performed within 72 hours . Complications: Shock , arrhythmias , ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome), renal failure , and DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) . Metabolic derangements like hypocalcemia , hyperglycemia , and hyperlipidemia may occur. Peripancreatic fluid collection , pancreatic abscess , pseudocyst , and pancreatic necrosis . Pleural effusion , pancreatic ascites , and pancreatic haemorrhage (pseudoaneurysm) are also common. Incorrect Options: Peptic ulcer disease (Option A) typically presents with epigastric pain, but it doesn't radiate to the back & does not cause elevated amylase and lipase levels. Acute cholecystitis (Option C) presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, often with fever and nausea, but it is not typically associated with marked increases in amylase and lipase. This condition would usually show elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. Pyogenic liver abscess (Option D) can present with fever and abdominal pain, but it does not typically cause significant increases in amylase and lipase. This condition would be more likely to show abnormal liver function tests and may be associated with other findings like fever or jaundice. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ea4781692777192e02222d4e1">Mite Explanation: The child’s symptoms of severe nocturnal itching and the presence of burrows in intertriginous areas, axillae, umbilicus, and between the fingers are characteristic of scabies, which is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei (a mite). Scabies: Parasitic infection of the skin caused by Sarcoptes scabiei (itch mite). Mode of spread: Scabies are highly contagious, and transmission is by skin-to-skin contact and fomites. Risk factors include poor personal hygiene. Clinical manifestation: The characteristic sign of scabies is the presence of burrows, Are thin, grayish-white or skin-colored, linear or wavy lines found in areas like the webbing between fingers, wrists, elbows, armpits, waistline, buttocks, genital area, and ankles, causing intense itching, especially at night. Examination typically reveals excoriated papules, typically over the web spaces of the fingers (as shown in the image). ommonly used radioactive isotope in teletherapy, a type of external beam radiotherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays, which are effective for treating deep-seated tumors.

Teletherapy (External beam radiation)

  • It is a form of radiation therapy in which the radiation source is placed at a distance from the body, delivering high-energy radiation beams to treat tumors.
  • External beam sources are:
    • Betatron
    • Cobalt
    • Linear accelerator
    • Neutron beam
    • Photon beam
    • Proton beam
    • Spray radiation
    • Stereotactic radiosurgery such as gamma knife
    • X-ray

Types of Beams

Electrons
  • Negatively charged particles
  • Limited penetration
  • Effective for tumors near the body surface (Skin tumors)

Photons

  • Can reach deep tumors
  • Scatter radiation along the path
  • Continue through normal tissue after reaching the tumor
  • Made up of high energy:
    • X-rays (LINAC- Linear accelerators)
    • Gamma rays

Protons
  • Positively charged particles
  • No radiation scatter
  • Stop precisely at the tumor location

 

cobalt 60 (Co60)

Linear accelerator
  • The Cobalt machine produces an artificial radioisotope (Co )
  • Advantage: Relative constancy of beam output
  • Source replacement approximately every 4 to 5 years
  • LINAC- Linear accelerators do not need a radioisotope
  • The fast-moving electron beam generates radiation which is used in radiotherapy
  • X-ray beams are produced

Advantages of External Beam

  • Painless
  • Do not require a hospital stay in most patients
  • Most patients can continue with their normal daily activities
  • Non-invasive

Iridium-192 (Option A): Used in brachytherapy, especially for treating cancers of the cervix, breast, and prostate.

Iodine-125 (Option B): Used in brachytherapy, particularly for prostate cancer and eye plaques (e.g., choroidal melanoma).

Iodine-131 (Option D): Used in the treatment of thyroid cancer and hyperthyroidism but not in teletherapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following provides valuable information about the reproductive behavior of couples within a population?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following provides valuable information about the reproductive behavior of couples within a population?
questions.solution: rong> The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is the average number of children born to a woman over her reproductive lifetime (15-49 years), usually expressed per woman. It is a common measure used to assess fertility levels within a population. TFR takes into account the age-specific fertility rates of women across all reproductive ages. TFR provides valuable information about the reproductive behavior of couples within a population and is used by demographers and policymakers to understand trends in population growth, as well as to formulate policies related to family planning, healthcare, and social services. Incorrect Options: NRR (Option B): Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) is the number of daughters or girls a newborn girl will bear or will have throughout her reproductive lifespan, considering the current age-specific fertility patterns and mortality rates. NRR is a mortality dependent fertility indicator. GFR (Option C): General Fertility Rate (GFR ) is the total number of live births in an area in a year per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) in a year. Not everyone in the reproductive age group is exposed to the risk of childbirth. GRR (Option D): Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR) is the total number of girls a woman will have throughout her reproductive age, considering the current age-specific fertility pattern and with out mortality. · GRR is given by TFR for girl children. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Blood cholesterol shown as mg/ml value is in which scale?
questions.stemHtml: Blood cholesterol shown as mg/ml value is in which scale?
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: Continuous data refers to data that can take any value within a given range and can be measured with a high degree of precision. Continuous data can include decimal values and can theoretically take on an infinite number of possible values within the specified range. Examples of continuous data include height, weight, temperature, and blood cholesterol levels (measured in mg/dL or mmol/L). In the context of blood cholesterol levels, they are measured on a continuous scale because they can take on any value within a range (e.g., from 100 mg/dL to 300 mg/dL) and can be measured with a high degree of precision using laboratory methods. Incorrect Options: Ordinal (Option A): Ordinal data refers to data that have a defined order or ranking but the differences between the values are not meaningful or consistent. For example, ranking students based on their exam scores (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.) represents ordinal data because while there is a ranking order, the difference in scores between students may not be uniform or meaningful. Nominal (Option B): Nominal data refers to categorical data where the categories are unordered and have no inherent numerical value. For example, colors (red, blue, green) or types of fruits (apple, banana, orange) represent nominal data because there is no inherent order or ranking among the categories. Discrete (Option C): Discrete data refers to data that can only take specific, distinct values and cannot take on values between these points. Discrete data are usually counts of items or events and are typically represented by whole numbers. For example, the number of students in a classroom or the number of cars in a parking lot are examples of discrete data. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with a testicular mass, and a gross image of the mass is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with a testicular mass, and a gross image of the mass is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: , with a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface and no signs of haemorrhage or necrosis, is most consistent with a diagnosis of Seminoma . It is the most common germ cell tumour of the testis. A similar presentation in the ovary is called dysgerminoma , and germinoma is present in the pineal gland . Incidence: Peak incidence in the fourth decade. Genetics: Seminomas contain isochromosome 12p and express OCT3/4 & NANOG. Gross: Seminoma has a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of haemorrhage or necrosis. Generally, the tunica albuginea is not penetrated, but extension to the epididymis, spermatic cord, or scrotal sac occasionally occurs. {{caption_text}} Histology of seminoma : It consists of sheets of monomorphic cells arranged in poorly defined lobules, separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytic (T cell) infiltration. Classic seminoma cells are large, round to polyhedral, with distinct membranes, central nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is clear or watery containing glycogen. {{caption_text}} Teratoma (Option A) are germ cell tumours containing tissues from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm). They can be benign (mature) or malignant (immature) and are commonly found in the testes, ovaries, or midline. Histologically, they present as heterogeneous masses with various tissue types (e.g., neural, muscle, epidermis, cartilage, thyroid, or intestinal tissue), often showing necrosis, calcification, or hair/teeth/bone. {{caption_text}} Yolk sac tumor (Option C ) is a malignant germ cell tumour, commonly found in the testes or ovaries, especially in children and young adults. It produces alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and appears as a solid mass with haemorrhage and necrosis, presenting in younger patients, particularly in the first two years of life. Microscopically, show a lace-like network of cuboidal or spindled cells with Schiller-Duval bodies and eosinophilic globules containing α-fetoprotein (AFP). {{caption_text}} Choriocarcinoma (Option D) is a rare, highly malignant germ cell tumour, typically in the testes, ovaries, or placenta, that secretes hCG. It presents with pain, swelling, and elevated hCG levels, often with haemorrhage, necrosis, and mixed trophoblastic cells. Microscopically, it contains syncytiotrophoblasts (multinucleated, hCG-containing) and cytotrophoblasts (polygonal, clear cytoplasm). {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: > Explanation: Based on the clinical features (non-pulsatile, stable size, and positive slip sign), this is most likely a lipoma , which is a benign tumour of fatty tissue. If the patient requests excision, and if there are no concerns about malignancy, excision can be performed to remove the lipoma for cosmetic or symptomatic reasons. Lipoma: A lipoma is a benign tumour composed of mature adipocytes (fat cells) and is the most common soft tissue tumor. These tumors are generally soft, mobile, and painless masses found beneath the skin. Most frequently found on the trunk, shoulders, neck, and arms. Histologically, lipomas consist of mature fat cells that are identical to normal adipose tissue but are encapsulated by a thin fibrous capsule , distinguishing them from the surrounding tissue. Lipomas are typically slow-growing, soft, and non-tender. They are usually asymptomatic but can cause discomfort if they compress nearby structures or are located in a site prone to friction or pressure. On physical examination, lipomas are well-circumscribed, mobile masses that can vary in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres. Slip sign: Positive Very low risk of malignant transformation into liposarcoma. (Option A) Management: Most lipomas do not require treatment unless they become symptomatic, grow rapidly, or cause cosmetic concerns. Surgical excision is the definitive treatment and is usually curative. Liposuction may also be an option for larger lipomas, but complete excision is preferred to prevent recurrence. While FNAC can be used for diagnosing soft tissue masses, it is not always required if the lesion's clinical presentation is typical of a lipoma. In many cases, a clinical diagnosis based on history and examination (such as soft, mobile, non-tender mass) is sufficient. (Option B) PET scans are generally used for staging known malignancies, such as lymphoma or other aggressive cancers. In this case, there is no indication that this is a malignant lesion, so a PET scan is unnecessary. (Option C) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: During laparoscopic surgery, while inserting the trocar, which of the following is most prone to injury?
questions.stemHtml: During laparoscopic surgery, while inserting the trocar, which of the following is most prone to injury?

options.label: C
options.text: Both superior and inferior epigastric arteries

questions.answerText: Both superior and inferior epigastric arteries
questions.solution: Both the superior and inferior epigastric arteries are at the highest risk during trocar placement due to their superficial and relatively consistent anatomical location in the anterior abdominal wall. The superior and inferior epigastric arteries run vertically within the posterior rectus sheath along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle . This creates a high-risk zone for injury during trocar insertion, especially in the lower abdomen . The superior epigastric artery descends from the internal thoracic artery , while the inferior epigastric artery ascends from the external iliac artery . These arteries anastomose within the rectus muscle. Their consistent anatomical location and superficial course within the anterior abdominal wall make them particularly vulnerable to injury when a trocar is placed incorrectly. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary identification made by a CBNAAT/ gene expert?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the primary identification made by a CBNAAT/ gene expert?
questions.solution: ge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) or GeneXpert is a molecular diagnostic tool that is primarily used for the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and for identifying rifampicin resistance . Rifampicin resistance is a key indicator for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) , which is a major concern in TB management. The GeneXpert system detects MTB DNA and also tests for rifampicin resistance by identifying mutations in the rpoB gene of the bacteria, which are responsible for resistance to this drug. TB lab investigations: Investigations Purpose Advantages Limitations Sputum smear Initial screening for pulmonary TB. Samples are stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen method or Auramine-O stain to visualize acid-fast bacilli (AFB) under a microscope. Quick and inexpensive. Can provide results within a few hours. Low sensitivity, especially in cases of extrapulmonary TB or in patients with HIV. Cannot differentiate between Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). Culture Methods Confirm the diagnosis of TB and assess drug susceptibility. Solid Media: Sputum is inoculated onto solid culture media like Löwenstein-Jensen or Middlebrook agar. Liquid Media: Automated systems like BACTEC or MGIT are used to detect growth faster. The gold standard for TB diagnosis. Allows for drug susceptibility testing. Time-consuming; results can take weeks. Requires specialized laboratory facilities. Xpert MTB/RIF Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. Method : A cartridge-based system that performs nucleic acid amplification (NAAT). Sputum or other specimens are processed directly in the cartridge. Rapid results (within 2 hours). High sensitivity and specificity. Simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance. More expensive than smear microscopy. Does not provide full drug susceptibility testing. LAMP (Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification) Detects DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Method : Amplifies DNA at a constant temperature without the need for thermal cycling. Sputum or other specimens are used. Rapid results (within 1-2 hours). High specificity and sensitivity. Can be performed at the point of care. Used for patients with HIV with CD4+ counts of less than 100 cells/μL irrespective of signs and symptoms of TB. Less widely available than PCR-based tests. Cannot detect drug resistance directly. TrueNat Point-of-care test for TB detection. Method : Uses a micro-PCR technology to amplify DNA. Results are available within 60 minutes. Portable and easy to use in peripheral health facilities. Provides results quickly, facilitating immediate treatment decisions. Line Probe Assay (LPA) Detects TB and drug resistance (rifampicin and isoniazid). Method : Sputum samples are processed, and DNA is extracted. Amplified DNA is hybridized to specific probes on a membrane strip. Rapid results (within 1-2 days). Can detect multiple mutations associated with drug resistance. Requires a laboratory setup and trained personnel. Not suitable for all strains of TB. RFLP IS6110 restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis is widely used for molecular epidemiological studies of tuberculosis. Restriction enzymes Nru I, EcoN I, Pst I, and Pvu II were used to analyze IS6110 fingerprints in Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains H37Rv (virulent) and H37Ra (avirulent). Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option A) : While the GeneXpert can detect MTB, the test is primarily used for identifying rifampicin resistance in addition to detecting the bacterium itself. MTB + Isoniazid (Option C) : While isoniazid resistance can be important in TB treatment, CBNAAT/GeneXpert is not specifically designed to detect isoniazid resistance ; it's more focused on rifampicin resistance . MTB + Ethambutol (Option D) : Similar to isoniazid, ethambutol resistance is not typically tested for by GeneXpert. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) or GeneXpert is a molecular diagnostic tool that is primarily used for the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) and for identifying rifampicin resistance. Rifampicin resistance is a key indicator for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), which is a major concern in TB management. The GeneXpert system detects MTB DNA and also tests for rifampicin resistance by identifying mutations in the rpoB gene of the bacteria, which are responsible for resistance to this drug.

TB lab investigations:

Investigations

Purpose

Advantages

Limitations

Sputum smear

  • Initial screening for pulmonary TB.
  • Samples are stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen method or Auramine-O stain to visualize acid-fast bacilli (AFB) under a microscope.
  • Quick and inexpensive. Can provide results within a few hours.
  • Low sensitivity, especially in cases of extrapulmonary TB or in patients with HIV.
  • Cannot differentiate between Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM).

Culture Methods
  • Confirm the diagnosis of TB and assess drug susceptibility.
  • Solid Media: Sputum is inoculated onto solid culture media like Löwenstein-Jensen or Middlebrook agar.
  • Liquid Media: Automated systems like BACTEC or MGIT are used to detect growth faster.
  • The gold standard for TB diagnosis.
  • Allows for drug susceptibility testing.
  • Time-consuming; results can take weeks.
  • Requires specialized laboratory facilities.

Xpert MTB/RIF
  • Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance.
  • Method:
  • A cartridge-based system that performs nucleic acid amplification (NAAT).
  • Sputum or other specimens are processed directly in the cartridge.
  • Rapid results (within 2 hours).
  • High sensitivity and specificity.
  • Simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance.
  • More expensive than smear microscopy.
  • Does not provide full drug susceptibility testing.

LAMP (Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification)
  • Detects DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Method:
  • Amplifies DNA at a constant temperature without the need for thermal cycling.
  • Sputum or other specimens are used.
  • Rapid results (within 1-2 hours).
  • High specificity and sensitivity.
  • Can be performed at the point of care.
  • Used for patients with HIV with CD4+ counts of less than 100 cells/μL irrespective of signs and symptoms of TB.
  • Less widely available than PCR-based tests.
  • Cannot detect drug resistance directly.

TrueNat
  • Point-of-care test for TB detection.
  • Method:
  • Uses a micro-PCR technology to amplify DNA.
  • Results are available within 60 minutes.
  • Portable and easy to use in peripheral health facilities.
  • Provides results quickly, facilitating immediate treatment decisions.

 

Line Probe Assay (LPA)

 
  • Detects TB and drug resistance (rifampicin and isoniazid).
  • Method:
    • Sputum samples are processed, and DNA is extracted.
    • Amplified DNA is hybridized to specific probes on a membrane strip.
  • Rapid results (within 1-2 days).
  • Can detect multiple mutations associated with drug resistance.
  • Requires a laboratory setup and trained personnel.
  • Not suitable for all strains of TB.

RFLP
  • IS6110 restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis is widely used for molecular epidemiological studies of tuberculosis.
  • Restriction enzymes Nru I, EcoN I, Pst I, and Pvu II were used to analyze IS6110 fingerprints in Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains H37Rv (virulent) and H37Ra (avirulent).

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option A): While the GeneXpert can detect MTB, the test is primarily used for identifying rifampicin resistance in addition to detecting the bacterium itself.

MTB + Isoniazid (Option C): While isoniazid resistance can be important in TB treatment, CBNAAT/GeneXpert is not specifically designed to detect isoniazid resistance; it's more focused on rifampicin resistance.

MTB + Ethambutol (Option D): Similar to isoniazid, ethambutol resistance is not typically tested for by GeneXpert.

questions.stem: A Patient who has a pet dog at home complains of hypochondrial pain. Radiological imaging shows a multilocular cyst within the liver. The organism involved is?
questions.stemHtml: A Patient who has a pet dog at home complains of hypochondrial pain. Radiological imaging shows a multilocular cyst within the liver. The organism involved is?
questions.solution: ings of a multilocular cyst in the liver, strongly suggest an infection with Echinococcus granulosus , which causes hydatid disease . Echinococcus granulosus Other name Dog tapeworm Definitive Host Dog (optimal host), wolf, jackal and fox Intermediate Host Sheep and cattle Accidental Intermediate Host Man (Harbors larval stage, not adult form) Infective Form Embryonated egg Mode of Infection Ingestion of the eggs due to: Intimate handling of infected dogs Eating raw vegetables or other food items contaminated with dog feces Eggs Ovoid in shape and brown in color Contains an embryo with three pairs of hooklets Larva Represent structure of scolex of adult worm and remains invaginated within a vesicular body. Adult Worm Consist of scolex, a short neck and strobila Scolex is pyriform, with four suckers and prominent rostellum bearing two circular rows of hooklets. Life Cycle: {{caption_text}} Hydatid Cyst Hydatid cysts are parasitic cysts caused by Echinococcus granulosus. Commonly Affected Organs Liver (most common site, about 60-70% of cases) Lungs (second most common site) Other organs (rare but possible): Brain, spleen, kidneys, bones, and peritoneum Clinical Features: Asymptomatic Phase: Common due to slow cyst growth. Symptomatic Phase: Liver Involvement: Mostly right lobe; Abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, obstructive jaundice, portal hypertension. Lung Involvement: Cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, pneumothorax. Layers of a hydatid cyst Layer Name Origin Description Main Function Outer Layer Pericyst Host-derived Thick fibrous layer created by the host's inflammatory response around the cyst. Eventually it develops into a dense fibrous capsule which may even calcify. Provides structural support and isolates the cyst from surrounding tissues. Middle Layer Ectocyst (Laminated Membrane) Parasite-derived Acellular,chitinous, laminated hyaline layer secreted by the parasite. Has the appearance of the white of a hard boiled egg. Acts as a barrier against host immune cells and protects the inner germinal layer. Inner Layer Endocyst (Germinal Layer) Parasite-derived Thin cellular layer lining the cyst interior. Consist of a number of nuclei embedded in a protoplasmic mass. Vital layer of the cyst. Site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices. Also secrete hydatid fluid, which fills the cyst. Entamoeba histolytica (Option B) : This protozoan causes amoebic liver abscesses , which can also lead to right upper quadrant pain. However, the cysts in amoebic infections are typically unilocular , not multilocular, and are usually associated with a history of dysentery or diarrhea . Strongyloides stercoralis (Option C) : This is a parasitic roundworm that causes strongyloidiasis and may lead to abdominal pain and diarrhea. However, it does not typically cause multilocular cysts in the liver. Ancylostoma duodenale (Option D) : This hookworm is associated with hookworm infection , causing symptoms like anemia and abdominal discomfort , but it does not lead to liver cysts. @Neet_pg_bot

ings of a multilocular cyst in the liver, strongly suggest an infection with Echinococcus granulosus, which causes hydatid disease.

Echinococcus granulosus

Other name

Dog tapeworm

Definitive Host

Dog (optimal host), wolf, jackal and fox

Intermediate Host

Sheep and cattle

Accidental Intermediate Host

Man (Harbors larval stage, not adult form)

Infective Form

Embryonated egg

Mode of Infection

Ingestion of the eggs due to:

  • Intimate handling of infected dogs
  • Eating raw vegetables or other food items contaminated with dog feces

Eggs

  • Ovoid in shape and brown in color
  • Contains an embryo with three pairs of hooklets

Larva

Represent structure of scolex of adult worm and remains invaginated within a vesicular body.

Adult Worm
  • Consist of scolex, a short neck and strobila
  • Scolex is pyriform, with four suckers and prominent rostellum bearing two circular rows of hooklets.

                                                Life Cycle:

 

Hydatid Cyst

Hydatid cysts are parasitic cysts caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

Commonly Affected Organs

  • Liver (most common site, about 60-70% of cases)
  • Lungs (second most common site)
  • Other organs (rare but possible): Brain, spleen, kidneys, bones, and peritoneum

Clinical Features:

  • Asymptomatic Phase: Common due to slow cyst growth.
  • Symptomatic Phase:
    • Liver Involvement: Mostly right lobe; Abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, obstructive jaundice, portal hypertension.
    • Lung Involvement: Cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, pneumothorax.

Layers of a hydatid cyst

Layer

Name

Origin

Description

Main Function

Outer Layer

Pericyst

Host-derived
  • Thick fibrous layer created by the host's inflammatory response around the cyst.
  • Eventually it develops into a dense fibrous capsule which may even calcify.

Provides structural support and isolates the cyst from surrounding tissues.

Middle Layer

Ectocyst (Laminated Membrane)

Parasite-derived
  • Acellular,chitinous, laminated hyaline layer secreted by the parasite.
  • Has the appearance of the white of a hard boiled egg.

Acts as a barrier against host immune cells and protects the inner germinal layer.

Inner Layer

Endocyst (Germinal Layer)

Parasite-derived
  • Thin cellular layer lining the cyst interior.
  • Consist of a number of nuclei embedded in a protoplasmic mass.
  • Vital layer of the cyst.
  • Site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.
  • Also secrete hydatid fluid, which fills the cyst.

Entamoeba histolytica (Option B): This protozoan causes amoebic liver abscesses, which can also lead to right upper quadrant pain. However, the cysts in amoebic infections are typically unilocular, not multilocular, and are usually associated with a history of dysentery or diarrhea.

Strongyloides stercoralis (Option C): This is a parasitic roundworm that causes strongyloidiasis and may lead to abdominal pain and diarrhea. However, it does not typically cause multilocular cysts in the liver.

Ancylostoma duodenale (Option D): This hookworm is associated with hookworm infection, causing symptoms like anemia and abdominal discomfort, but it does not lead to liver cysts.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought with complaints of headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness for a few days. He had undergone a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for hydrocephalus a year ago. What is the most common cause of shunt malfunction in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought with complaints of headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness for a few days. He had undergone a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for hydrocephalus a year ago. What is the most common cause of shunt malfunction in this patient?
questions.solution: t obstruction Explanation: Shunt obstruction is the most common cause of VP shunt malfunction. This can occur anywhere along the length of the shunt, but it often happens at the distal catheter (the part of the shunt that drains into the peritoneum). A Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is generally considered for long-term management of hydrocephalus . It is implanted surgically to divert excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the ventricles of the brain to the peritoneal cavity , where it can be absorbed by the body. Management of Hydrocephalus: Medical : Acetazolamide and furosemide can temporarily reduce CSF production but are not effective long-term. Surgical: (CSF Diversion) Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt: Valved tubing from the ventricle to the peritoneal cavity. Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy: It is a useful treatment for certain cases of hydrocephalus, especially when there is an obstructive pattern that can be bypassed surgically and not always suitable for all patients and is considered an alternative to shunt placement Intrauterine Treatment : Results are generally poor except in cases associated with fetal meningomyelocele. Complications: Shunt occlusion (headache, papilledema, vomiting, altered mental status) and bacterial infection leading to meningitis/peritonitis (fever, headache, meningismus), typically caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

Shunt obstruction is the most common cause of VP shunt malfunction. This can occur anywhere along the length of the shunt, but it often happens at the distal catheter (the part of the shunt that drains into the peritoneum).

A Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is generally considered for long-term management of hydrocephalus. It is implanted surgically to divert excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the ventricles of the brain to the peritoneal cavity, where it can be absorbed by the body.

Management of Hydrocephalus:

  • Medical: Acetazolamide and furosemide can temporarily reduce CSF production but are not effective long-term.
  • Surgical: (CSF Diversion)
    • Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt: Valved tubing from the ventricle to the peritoneal cavity.
    • Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy: It is a useful treatment for certain cases of hydrocephalus, especially when there is an obstructive pattern that can be bypassed surgically and not always suitable for all patients and is considered an alternative to shunt placement
  • Intrauterine Treatment: Results are generally poor except in cases associated with fetal meningomyelocele.

Complications: Shunt occlusion (headache, papilledema, vomiting, altered mental status) and bacterial infection leading to meningitis/peritonitis (fever, headache, meningismus), typically caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the condition that presents with an empty delta sign.
questions.solution: eta" data-dictid="f7d3133242169277718518c059ad55">delta sign is a radiological finding seen on contrast-enhanced CT scans or MR venography. It indicates the presence of a thrombus in the dural venous sinus, most commonly the superior sagittal sinus. The thrombus appears as a filling defect surrounded by contrast enhancement, forming a triangular or delta-shaped void. Central venous sinus thrombosis CVT should be suspected in patients presenting with headaches, seizures, or encephalopathy. Can occur in superficial or deep dural venous sinuses, affecting either isolated veins or as part of broader venous sinus thrombosis. Factors like intracranial infections , trauma, dehydration, pregnancy , oral contraceptives , smoking, and vasculitis (e.g., Behçet disease) can trigger CVT. If absent, a thrombophilia screening is necessary. CT Findings : {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} The empty delta sign , visible in contrast-enhanced CT scans, indicates dural venous sinus thrombosis in the superior sagittal sinus as a triangular filling defect outlined by contrast, representing a thrombus. The dense vein sign , a hyperdense vessel sign indicating hyperattenuating thrombus due to acute venous thrombosis, is found in cortical veins or dural venous sinuses . MRI Findings : {{caption_text}} Loss of normal flow void; thrombosed vessels may appear hyperintense on T1 and T2 sequences. Very acute thrombus can be hypointense on T2, mimicking flow voids. SWI (Susceptibility Weighted Imaging) can highlight thrombosed veins and detect acute hemorrhage. questions.stem: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out lung and contralateral tracheal deviation. In which of the following conditions is this seen?
questions.stemHtml: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out lung and contralateral tracheal deviation. In which of the following conditions is this seen?
questions.solution: g> Explanation: The radiological findings indicate a tracheal deviation to the side opposite to the white-out lung field due to a thoracic mass (mainly due to massive pleural effusion) . This pattern occurs when a space-occupying lesion or massive fluid collection (such as due to a lung cancer) in the thoracic cavity creates enough mass effect to push the mediastinal structures away from the affected side. {{caption_text}} The pleural fluid is seen as opacity (single large black arrow) with lateral upward sloping of a meniscus- shaped contour. The right diaphragmatic contour is also completely obliterated, indicating presence of fluid in the right pleural space. In spite of a moderately large right pleural effusion , the trachea appears to be slightly shifted to the right side (as depicted by small black arrows) indicating an underlying lung pathology on the right side. Pneumothorax (Option A) typically presents with a hyperlucent lung field without vascular markings due to air collection in the pleural space. In this X-ray, we see opacity rather than hyperlucency. Consolidation (Option B) shows haziness or opacity on X-ray but maintains some visualization of underlying vascular markings. A complete white-out appearance is not typical. Furthermore, significant tracheal deviation is not a characteristic feature of simple consolidation. Collapse of the lung (Option C) would show tracheal deviation toward the same side as the opacity, not away from it. This is because collapse creates negative pressure that pulls the mediastinal structures toward the affected side. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a recent travel history to Africa presents with fever, confusion and neurological deficits. Laboratory analysis reveals the following findings. This organism exhibits a specific property that facilitates sequestration in vascular beds to avoid splenic clearance. What is the phenomenon called?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with a recent travel history to Africa presents with fever, confusion and neurological deficits. Laboratory analysis reveals the following findings. This organism exhibits a specific property that facilitates sequestration in vascular beds to avoid splenic clearance. What is the phenomenon called?
questions.solution: ong> The patient’s symptoms, including fever, confusion, and neurological deficits, along with the travel history to Africa, suggest a Plasmodium falciparum infection, which is the causative agent of severe malaria . Plasmodium falciparum has a specific property that facilitates its sequestration in the microvasculature, especially in organs like the brain (leading to cerebral malaria), by adhering to the endothelial cells of blood vessels. This process is known as cytoadherence . Plasmodium falciparum is the primary species associated with cytoadherence , where infected red blood cells adhere to endothelial cells in blood vessels. This leads to complications like cerebral malaria due to vessel blockage and reduced blood flow. Pathogenesis of Malignant Malaria: Cytoadherence: In Plasmodium falciparum malaria , late-stage schizonts secrete proteins that create knob-like protrusions on the surfaces of infected RBCs. This results in the expression of the adhesive protein PfEMP-1 (P. falciparum Erythrocyte Membrane Protein) , which makes the infected RBCs sticky. Inflammatory cytokines, particularly IFN-γ, enhance the expression of endothelial receptors such as thrombospondin, E-selectin, VCAM-1, and ICAM-1 in the brain, chondroitin sulfate B in the placenta, and CD36 in most other organs. These receptors promote the cytoadherence of infected RBCs to the endothelium , leading to blockage of capillaries and venules. Rosette formation: Infected RBCs can adhere to uninfected RBCs , forming rosettes . Auto-Agglutination: The phenomenon where parasitised red blood cells (RBCs) clump together These mechanisms cause capillary plugging and reduced microcirculation in vital organs, including the brain, kidneys, lungs, spleen, intestines, bone marrow, and placenta, resulting in severe complications like cerebral malaria. Other notable virulence factors: Histidine-rich protein II (HRP II) Glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) Rosetting (Option A) : This refers to the formation of clusters of uninfected red blood cells around an infected red blood cell. It is a phenomenon observed in Plasmodium falciparum infections, but cytoadherence is the more accurate term for the process responsible for sequestration in the microvasculature. Agglutination (Option B) : This refers to the clumping of cells or particles, typically used to describe antibody-antigen interactions. It is not related to the sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in malaria. Schizogony (Option D) : This is the asexual reproductive process of Plasmodium , during which the parasite undergoes multiple rounds of division inside red blood cells. It is a key part of the parasite's life cycle but does not describe the sequestration mechanism that causes the clinical manifestations seen in malaria. @Neet_pg_bot

Cytoadherence:

  • In Plasmodium falciparum malaria, late-stage schizonts secrete proteins that create knob-like protrusions on the surfaces of infected RBCs. This results in the expression of the adhesive protein PfEMP-1 (P. falciparum Erythrocyte Membrane Protein), which makes the infected RBCs sticky.
  • Inflammatory cytokines, particularly IFN-γ, enhance the expression of endothelial receptors such as thrombospondin, E-selectin, VCAM-1, and ICAM-1 in the brain, chondroitin sulfate B in the placenta, and CD36 in most other organs. These receptors promote the cytoadherence of infected

  • RBCs to the endothelium, leading to blockage of capillaries and venules.

Auto-Agglutination: The phenomenon where parasitised red blood cells (RBCs) clump together

These mechanisms cause capillary plugging and reduced microcirculation in vital organs, including the brain, kidneys, lungs, spleen, intestines, bone marrow, and placenta, resulting in severe complications like cerebral malaria.

Other notable virulence factors:

  • Histidine-rich protein II (HRP II)
  • Glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)

It is a phenomenon observed in Plasmodium falciparum infections, but cytoadherence is the more accurate term for the process responsible for sequestration in the microvasculature.

Agglutination (Option B): This refers to the clumping of cells or particles, typically used to describe antibody-antigen interactions. It is not related to the sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in malaria.

Schizogony (Option D): This is the asexual reproductive process of Plasmodium, during which the parasite undergoes multiple rounds of division inside red blood cells. It is a key part of the parasite's life cycle but does not describe the sequestration mechanism that causes the clinical manifestations seen in malaria.

decreased glucose, and increased protein are characteristic of tuberculous meningitis, which is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB).

Tuberculous Meningitis

  • Tuberculous meningitis presents with a subacute course of headaches, mental changes, and fever over weeks, with CSF findings of lymphocyte predominance, elevated protein, and low glucose. Cobweb coagulum seen in CSF.

Cobweb coagulum

  • Cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus can occur.
  • AFB smear is often negative, and diagnosis may rely on culture or Xpert MTB/RIF assay.

TB Meningitis

Pathophysiology
  • Tuberculous Meningitis results from hematogenous spread of primary or postprimary TB or rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space.

Onset

Evolves over 1–2 weeks, slower than bacterial meningitis.

Symptoms
  • Early Symptoms
    • Headache, mild mental changes, low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia, irritability over several weeks.
  • Advanced Symptoms
    • Severe headache, confusion, lethargy, altered sensorium, neck rigidity, cranial nerve palsies (especially ocular). Can progress to coma, hydrocephalus, and intracranial hypertension.

Lumbar Puncture Findings (CSF)
  • High leukocyte count (up to 1000/μL), typically lymphocyte predominance
  • Protein: 1–8 g/L (100–800 mg/dL)
  • Low glucose concentration
  • AFB is rarely seen; repeated lumbar punctures increase yield.
  • CSF culture diagnostic in up to 80% (gold standard).

Xpert MTB/RIF Assay
  • Sensitivity up to 80%.
  • A negative result does not exclude TB.

Imaging
  • CT, MRI: Shows hydrocephalus and enhancement of basal cisterns or ependyma.

Basal cistern enhancement

  • In >50% of cases, old pulmonary lesions or military pattern on CXR.

Treatment

Immediate treatment with positive Xpert MTB/RIF.

  • Chemotherapy is effective but neurologic sequelae occur in 25% of cases, especially with delayed diagnosis.
  • Glucocorticoid Therapy
    • Dexamethasone reduces mortality and severe disability but may not prevent neurological sequelae.
    • Regimen: 0.4 mg/kg/day IV, tapering weekly, followed by oral tapering. WHO recommends tapering over 6–8 weeks.

Lymphocytosis (Option A): The presence of lymphocytes in the CSF suggests a chronic infection or inflammation, which is typical of tuberculous meningitis.

Decreased glucose (Option B): Low glucose levels in the CSF are a hallmark of tuberculous meningitis (as well as other forms of bacterial meningitis), as the bacteria consume glucose. This is often seen in tuberculosis-related infections.

Increased protein (Option C): Elevated protein levels in the CSF are also consistent with tuberculous meningitis, which causes an inflammatory response and protein leakage into the CSF.

CMV (cytomegalovirus)

Class

Betaherpesvirinae subfamily of the Herpesviridae family.

Modes of transmission
  • Oral route, respiratory & body secretions (most common)
  • Vertical transmission
  • Sexual transmission
  • Organ transplantation
  • Blood transfusion

Host cells
  • Salivary gland
  • Kidney

Clinical features

Congenital infection

  • Most common intrauterine infection with congenital defects.
  • Common presentation:
    • Petechiae
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Jaundice
  • Less common presentation:
    • Microcephaly
    • Cerebral calcifications
    • Intrauterine growth retardation
    • Prematurity
  • Other defects: Sensorineural hearing loss.

 

Perinatal infection

  • Commonly asymptomatic.
  • Occasionally, premature infants present with interstitial pneumonitis.

 

Immunocompromised

  • This is seen in AIDS, HIV, organ transplant patients and cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy.
  • Presentations in AIDS and HIV
    • CMV chorioretinitis
    • Progressive dementia,
    • Cranial nerve defects,
  • Presentations in Organ transplant
    • Bilateral interstitial pneumonia
    • Febrile leukopenia
    • Obliterative bronchiolitis
    • Graft atherosclerosis
    • Rejection of renal allografts.

 

Immunocompetent

  • Usually, it occurs following a blood transfusion.
  • It presents similar to infectious mononucleosis, but heterophile antibody tests would be negative.

Investigations

Peripheral smear: Owl’s eye appearance of inclusion bodies.

 

 

Virus isolation

It is done by

  • Human fibroblast cell line culture
  • Shell vial culture

 

Antigen detected: PP65

 

Antibody detection

It is done by ELISA, and the antibodies detected are

  • CMV IgM antibodies
  • CMV IgG antibodies
  • Against PP150 and PP65,
  • Against the PP52

 

PCR

  • Used in detecting CMV DNA
  • Quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) by PCR is the most sensitive and specific testing.

Treatment
  • Ganciclovir (Drug of choice)
  • Foscarnet (in Ganciclovir resistance)
  • CMV immunoglobulins and Ganciclovir are given to bone marrow transplant patients.

 

EBV (Epstein Barr virus) (Option A) primarily causes infectious mononucleosis, marked by fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue, and usually does not lead to pneumonia. Downey cells, or atypical lymphocytes, are large, vacuolated, and often display a ballerina skirt appearance.

 

Pox virus (Option C), like smallpox (eradicated) and molluscum contagiosum, causes skin lesions such as pustules or bumps. While they don't typically cause pneumonia, they can lead to systemic infections, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

Chickenpox (Option D), caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), leads to a rash of red spots and blisters. In immunocompromised patients, it can cause severe complications like varicella pneumonia, though less commonly than CMV or bacterial pneumonia, and may require antiviral treatment.

questions.stem: A lung cancer patient has hyperpigmentation of palmar and sole creases. Which of the following is responsible for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A lung cancer patient has hyperpigmentation of palmar and sole creases. Which of the following is responsible for this presentation?
questions.solution: ations indicate Ectopic Cushing's syndrome , a paraneoplastic syndrome commonly associated with lung cancer. Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) produced by the tumor is cleaved to form Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone (MSH) and ACTH , leading to hyperpigmentation. This process represents one of the most common hormonally-induced paraneoplastic syndromes in small cell lung cancer (SCLC).   • Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) produced by the tumor is cleaved to form Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone (MSH) and ACTH, leading to hyperpigmentation. This process represents one of the most common hormonally-induced paraneoplastic syndromes in small cell lung cancer (SCLC).

    • Ectopic Cushing's Syndrome

    Definition

    ACTH production from non-pituitary sources leading to Cushing's syndrome

    Epidemiology

    Accounts for 10-20% of cases of Cushing's syndrome

    Common Sources
    • Small cell lung cancer (most common)
    • Bronchial and thymic carcinoids
    • Islet tumors
    • Pheochromocytomas
    • Medullary thyroid carcinomas

    Pathophysiology
    • Increased expression of POMC gene from non-pituitary sources
    • Production of MSH, β-lipotropin, and other POMC-derived peptides
    • Production of ACTH fragments

    Clinical Features
    • Hyperglycemia
    • Marked fluid retention
    • Hyperpigmentation manifestations due to MSH
    • Less marked weight gain compared to pituitary Cushing's
    • Centripetal fat redistribution
    • Hypertension
    • Hypokalemia
    • Metabolic alkalosis
    • Glucose intolerance

    Diagnosis
    • Very high ACTH levels (typically >2-3 times normal)
    • No response to high-dose dexamethasone suppression

    Treatment
    • Treatment of underlying malignancy
    • Glucocorticoid receptor blockers
    • Steroidogenesis inhibitors
    • Management of complications (diabetes, hypokalemia)

    Key Distinctions from Pituitary Cushing's
    • Higher ACTH levels
    • No response to dexamethasone suppression
    • More rapid onset
    • More severe metabolic complications

    C-peptide (Option B) is a byproduct formed during the conversion of proinsulin to insulin. It has no role in the hyperpigmentation seen in paraneoplastic syndromes associated with lung cancer.

    Neuropeptide Y (Option C) is involved in appetite regulation through hypothalamic signaling. This peptide does not contribute to the hyperpigmentation observed in paraneoplastic syndromes.

    Melanin (Option D) is the end product of melanogenesis responsible for skin pigmentation. While it is the final pigment, the question asks about the hormone responsible for triggering the hyperpigmentation, which is MSH.

questions.stem: Which hormone increases during periods of stress, starvation, and deep sleep?
questions.stemHtml: Which hormone increases during periods of stress, starvation, and deep sleep?
questions.solution: ormone levels increase significantly during periods of deep sleep, stress, and starvation. This hormone, produced by the pituitary gland, is crucial for the body's repair and regeneration processes, which are most active during deep sleep. Additionally, growth hormone release is influenced by stress and nutritional status, with levels rising in response to these conditions to support the body's adaptive responses​ Factors controlling GH secretion and their effects Hypothalamic Control Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) : Increases GH synthesis and secretion. Somatostatin (GHIH) : Decreases GH secretion. Nutritional Factors Hypoglycemia : Promotes GH secretion to increase blood glucose levels and mobilize energy. Amino Acids : Stimulate GH release, supporting protein synthesis and growth. Starvation or Protein Deficiency : This leads to elevated GH levels to conserve body proteins and utilize fats as an energy source. Physiological Factors Exercise : Enhances GH secretion Sleep : GH surges during deep sleep are vital for growth and tissue repair processes. Stress : Physical and emotional stressors can increase GH secretion Hormonal Factors Ghrelin : Increases GH secretion and stimulates appetite. Sex Hormones (Estrogen and Testosterone) : Contribute to increased GH secretion during puberty, supporting growth and development. Negative Feedback Control : GH and IGF-1 levels feedback to inhibit further GH release, maintaining homeostasis and preventing excess GH production. Glucocorticoids (Option B): While glucocorticoids like cortisol do increase during stress, they do not typically increase during deep sleep. In fact, high cortisol levels can disrupt sleep. Cortisol (Option C): Cortisol levels increase during stress and early morning hours but not during deep sleep. Elevated cortisol at night is associated with poor sleep quality. Prolactin (Option D): Prolactin levels can rise during sleep, but its increase is not as pronounced or consistent in response to stress and starvation as growth hormone. @Neet_pg_bot

ormone levels increase significantly during periods of deep sleep, stress, and starvation.
