    • Factors controlling GH secretion and their effects

    Hypothalamic Control
    • Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH): Increases GH synthesis and secretion.
    • Somatostatin (GHIH): Decreases GH secretion.

    Nutritional Factors
    • Hypoglycemia: Promotes GH secretion to increase blood glucose levels and mobilize energy.
    • Amino Acids: Stimulate GH release, supporting protein synthesis and growth.
    • Starvation or Protein Deficiency: This leads to elevated GH levels to conserve body proteins and utilize fats as an energy source.

    Physiological Factors
    • Exercise: Enhances GH secretion
    • Sleep: GH surges during deep sleep are vital for growth and tissue repair processes.
    • Stress: Physical and emotional stressors can increase GH secretion

    Hormonal Factors
    • Ghrelin: Increases GH secretion and stimulates appetite.
    • Sex Hormones (Estrogen and Testosterone): Contribute to increased GH secretion during puberty, supporting growth and development.
    • Negative Feedback Control: GH and IGF-1 levels feedback to inhibit further GH release, maintaining homeostasis and preventing excess GH production.

    Glucocorticoids (Option B): While glucocorticoids like cortisol do increase during stress, they do not typically increase during deep sleep. In fact, high cortisol levels can disrupt sleep.

    Cortisol (Option C): Cortisol levels increase during stress and early morning hours but not during deep sleep. Elevated cortisol at night is associated with poor sleep quality.

    Prolactin (Option D): Prolactin levels can rise during sleep, but its increase is not as pronounced or consistent in response to stress and starvation as growth hormone.

    • Kala-azar/ Black sickness/Dum-dum fever/Sandfly disease/ Visceral Leishmaniasis

    Organism

    Protozoan

    Epidemiology

    Endemic in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal

    Types
    1. Visceral (Kala-Azar): L. donovani
    2. Cutaneous: L. tropica
    3. Mucocutaneous: L. braziliensis
    4. Post-kala-azar dermal (PKLD): Immune response

    Reservoir
    • Humans (non-zoonotic)

    Vector
    • Sandfly (Phlebotomus argentipes): has hairy wings.

    Environmental
    • Peak outbreak: November to April

    Mechanism of transmission
    • Bite of sandfly
    • Blood transfusion (rare)

    Incubation period
    • 10 days to 2 years. (1-4 months average)

    Clinical features
    • Visceral: Fever, Weight loss, Hepatosplenomegaly, Anemia.
    • Cutaneous: Painful skin ulcers
    • Mucocutaneous: Rapid mucosal destruction of nose and oropharynx
    • PKDL: Skin nodules filled with micro-organisms

    Diagnosis
    • Rapid diagnostic kits: rk39-dipstick test.
      • Used for field surveys.
    • Biopsy (Gold standard): Leishmania Donovan bodies (amastigotes)

    Sandfly control measures
    • DDT: 1-2gm/m2.
    • BHC (benzene hexachloride)

    Treatment
    • DOC: Single dose Liposomal amphotericin-B (LAMB)10 mg/kg
    • Alternatives:
      • Miltefosine + Paramomycin
      • Pentamidine

    Incorrect Options:

    Options A, B, and D are incorrect, as they do not show amastigotes (LD bodies) which are diagnostic.

questions.stemHtml: A young lady gave a history of unprotected intercourse four days back. She is requesting an emergency contraception. Which of the following is most suitable in this case?

>
  • The typical hand movements shown in the image are known as asterixis or "flapping tremors. These characteristic hand movements are seen in patients of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, potentially due to hypercarbia.

The 3 causes of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy include:

  • Hepatic encephalopathy (Increased level of ammonia)
  • Uremic encephalopathy (Increased level of urea)
  • Hypercarbia (Increased level of CO2)

This condition occurs frequently in patients with chronic CO2 retention, particularly those receiving oxygen therapy for emphysema or chronic pulmonary disease. The flapping movement is elicited by having patients extend their arms and bend their wrists back.

 

Thyrotoxicosis (Option A) presents with fine tremors. The tremor pattern is distinctly different from the coarse flapping movements seen in asterixis.

Hemiballismus (Option C) manifests with wild, flinging movements at the shoulder joint. These movements are abrupt and unilateral compared to the bilateral wrist movements seen in asterixis.

Hypoxia (Option D) typically causes disorientation and mental status changes with O2 saturation <90%. While it can cause neurological symptoms, it does not specifically produce the characteristic flapping tremor seen in this case.

Salter-Harris Classification of growth plate fractures: Type Description Treatment and Prognosis Type I (Option A) Separation of the physis (growth plate), without involvement of the metaphysis or epiphysis. Excellent prognosis if treated promptly Treated with immobilization and observation. Type II (Option B) Fracture through the physis and part of the metaphysis. The metaphyseal fragment is displaced, forming a triangle (known as the Thurston-Holland sign). Good prognosis with proper treatment. Treated with reduction and casting. Rarely affects future growth. Type III (Option C) Fracture through the physis and epiphysis, with the epiphysis displaced. May result in joint deformity or growth disturbance if not managed well. Surgical intervention required for proper alignment and fixation. Type IV Fracture through the physis, metaphysis, and epiphysis. Involves all three areas. Can lead to growth disturbances or joint deformity. Treatment typically involves surgical fixation. Type V (Option D) Crushing injury of the physis (growth plate), resulting in compression and loss of the growth plate. No fracture line visible. Risk of growth arrest and long-term deformities. Surgical intervention required. @Neet_pg_bot

Type

Crushing injury of the physis (growth plate), resulting in compression and loss of the growth plate. No fracture line visible.

questions.solution: his case, given the irregular enhancement and enlargement of the renal lesion on CECT, is Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC), making the origin of pain the kidney most likely. Clinical Features of Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC): Classic symptoms such as hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass - “ TOO - LATE” TRIAD seen in 10% of patients with advanced disease. Systemic symptoms like weight loss, fever, and fatigue can also occur. In advanced stages, RCC may metastasise to the lungs, bones, and brain. A non-reducing varicocele, referred to as a suspicious varicocele , may indicate the presence of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), often due to a thrombus originating from the left RCC. Treatment of RCC: RCCs are radio and chemo-resistant. Surgical Management: Partial Nephrectomy (Option A): Involves removing only the tumour while preserving the remainder of the kidney. Indications: T1 Disease(<7cm) Restricted to poles RCC in solitary functioning kidney Radical Nephrectomy: Involves removal of the kidney with Gerota’s fascia, para-aortic nodes, and ureter up to the pelvic brim. Indications: Larger tumours or when partial nephrectomy is not feasible Ablative Techniques Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA) and Cryoablation Involve destroying the tumor using extreme temperatures. Indications: Patients who are not surgical candidates Patients with small tumours (T1a lesions) (usually <4 cm).     • Systemic symptoms like weight loss, fever, and fatigue can also occur.
    • In advanced stages, RCC may metastasise to the lungs, bones, and brain.
    • A non-reducing varicocele, referred to as a suspicious varicocele, may indicate the presence of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), often due to a thrombus originating from the left RCC.

    Surgical Management:

    Targeted Therapy

It works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction, prolonging the action of acetylcholine and improving muscle strength. Uses of Neostigmine: Treatment of myasthenia gravis as it increases the availability of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, thereby improving muscle strength. To reverse the effects of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents after surgical procedures. In managing urinary retention due to its ability to stimulate bladder muscle contractions. Cobra bites because cobra toxin disrupts the neuromuscular junction, resulting in respiratory paralysis. Bethanechol (Option A) is a cholinergic agonist that stimulates muscarinic receptors, which are found primarily in the urinary and gastrointestinal tracts. It is not used to reverse muscle relaxation after surgery because it does not affect the neuromuscular junction. Atropine (Option B) is a direct-acting anticholinergic (muscarinic antagonist) , blocking the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. It is used to treat bradycardia and to prevent the effects of excessive acetylcholine release. However, it does not reverse muscle relaxation. Edrophonium (Option D) is a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and is used as a diagnostic tool in suspected cases of myasthenia gravis (Tensilon test). It is administered intravenously to individuals suspected of myasthenia gravis . It temporarily improves muscle strength, confirming the diagnosis by demonstrating impaired neuromuscular transmission due to acetylcholine receptor deficiency . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following mutations is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following mutations is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.solution: iladelphia chromosome is a balanced translocation between the long arm of chromosomes 9 and 22 [t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)] . It is present in the majority of patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). Formation of Philadelphia chromosome: A balanced translocation is a type of chromosomal rearrangement in which segments of two different chromosomes break and exchange places without any loss of genetic material. In the case of CML, a segment of chromosome 9 containing the ABL gene ( Abelson Leukemia) , located at the q34 region, moves to chromosome 22. Similarly, the segment of chromosome 22 containing the BCR gene (breakpoint cluster region) , located at the q11 region, moves to chromosome 9. This exchange results in the formation of two derivative chromosomes: one with the truncated chromosome 9 segment and the BCR-ABL fusion gene and the other with the truncated chromosome 22 segment. The chromosome containing the BCR-ABL fusion gene is known as the Philadelphia chromosome. {{caption_text}} The BCR-ABL fusion forms a novel oncoprotein called p210 bcr-abl-1 (210 = molecular weight in kiloDalton—210 kDa). Inversion (Option A) occurs when a segment of DNA breaks away from the chromosome, flips around, and reattaches in the reverse orientation. This is not the mechanism involved in Philadelphia chromosome formation. Insertion (Option B) involves the addition of extra nucleotides into a DNA sequence. This type of mutation can cause frameshift mutations but is not responsible for the Philadelphia chromosome. Deletion (Option D) results in the loss of a segment of DNA from a chromosome. While deletions are important mutations, they do not cause the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome, which involves an exchange of genetic material between chromosomes. @Neet_pg_bot

iladelphia chromosome is a balanced translocation between the long arm of chromosomes 9 and 22 [t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)]. It is present in the majority of patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).

Formation of Philadelphia chromosome:

  • A balanced translocation is a type of chromosomal rearrangement in which segments of two different chromosomes break and exchange places without any loss of genetic material.
  • In the case of CML, a segment of chromosome 9 containing the ABL gene (Abelson Leukemia), located at the q34 region, moves to chromosome 22.
  • Similarly, the segment of chromosome 22 containing the BCR gene (breakpoint cluster region), located at the q11 region, moves to chromosome 9.
  • This exchange results in the formation of two derivative chromosomes: one with the truncated chromosome 9 segment and the BCR-ABL fusion gene and the other with the truncated chromosome 22 segment.
  • The chromosome containing the BCR-ABL fusion gene is known as the Philadelphia chromosome.

 

  • The BCR-ABL fusion forms a novel oncoprotein called p210bcr-abl-1 (210 = molecular weight in kiloDalton—210 kDa).

Inversion (Option A) occurs when a segment of DNA breaks away from the chromosome, flips around, and reattaches in the reverse orientation. This is not the mechanism involved in Philadelphia chromosome formation.

Insertion (Option B) involves the addition of extra nucleotides into a DNA sequence. This type of mutation can cause frameshift mutations but is not responsible for the Philadelphia chromosome.

Deletion (Option D) results in the loss of a segment of DNA from a chromosome. While deletions are important mutations, they do not cause the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome, which involves an exchange of genetic material between chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazides in DCT?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazides in DCT?
questions.solution: exert their effects by inhibiting the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) of the nephron. Na-Cl symporter normally facilitates the reabsorption of Na+ and Cl- from the filtrate back into the bloodstream. By blocking this, thiazides reduce the reabsorption of Na+ and Cl- , leading to increased excretion of these ions in the urine. This results in diuresis and a reduction in blood volume , helping to lower blood pressure and reduce edema (associated with CHF, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, chronic renal failure, acute glomerulonephritis) Blockade of Na Cl symporter (Option A) : This is the mechanism of action of loop diuretics (like furosemide ), which inhibit the Na-K-2Cl symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, not the distal convoluted tubule. Blockade of aldosterone receptors (Option C) : This describes the mechanism of aldosterone antagonists (like spironolactone ), which block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct and distal tubule, leading to increased sodium excretion and potassium retention. Blockade of epithelial sodium channels (Option D) : This refers to the action of amiloride , which is a potassium-sparing diuretic . They block the epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and collect the duct , reducing sodium reabsorption and preventing potassium loss. @Neet_pg_bot

  • By blocking this, thiazides reduce the reabsorption of Na+ and Cl-, leading to increased excretion of these ions in the urine.
  • This results in diuresis and a reduction in blood volume, helping to lower blood pressure and reduce edema (associated with CHF, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, chronic renal failure, acute glomerulonephritis)

    • Blockade of Na Cl symporter (Option A): This is the mechanism of action of loop diuretics (like furosemide), which inhibit the Na-K-2Cl symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, not the distal convoluted tubule.

    Blockade of aldosterone receptors (Option C): This describes the mechanism of aldosterone antagonists (like spironolactone), which block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct and distal tubule, leading to increased sodium excretion and potassium retention.

questions.stem: A teenager was brought to the OPD with complaints of delayed fertility and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination reveals a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Which karyotype is associated with a given condition?
questions.stemHtml: A teenager was brought to the OPD with complaints of delayed fertility and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination reveals a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Which karyotype is associated with a given condition?
questions.solution: l> The teenager presenting with delayed fertility, primary amenorrhea, a webbed neck, and widely spaced nipples is diagnosed with Turner Syndrome , which is characterised by the karyotype 45, X (monosomy X) . It is characterised by complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome, leading to hypogonadism in phenotypic females. Clinical features: Short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema, and primary amenorrhea. The image below shows karyotyping in Turner syndrome. {{caption_text}} 47, XXY (Option B) is Klinefelter syndrome , which occurs in males with an extra X chromosome, leading to hypogonadism, small testes, gynecomastia, reduced body/facial hair, and infertility. While it is associated with tall stature and sometimes mild intellectual disabilities, it does not present with features like a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, or primary amenorrhea, which are characteristic of Turner syndrome. 47, XXX (Option C) is Triple X Syndrome , which occurs in females with an extra X chromosome. It is usually asymptomatic or causes mild developmental delays but does not present with primary amenorrhea or webbed neck, which are typical of Turner syndrome. 47, XYY (Option D) is Jacob's Syndrome , which occurs in males with an extra Y chromosome, leading to tall stature and mild intellectual disabilities, but it does not cause primary amenorrhea, webbed neck, or widely spaced nipples, which are characteristic of Turner syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Dynein protein is an example of?
questions.stemHtml: Dynein protein is an example of?
questions.solution: p> Dynein is best classified as a transport protein . It is a motor protein that moves along microtubules in cells, transporting cellular cargo toward the minus end of these structures. This function is essential for various intracellular transport processes, including the movement of organelles, vesicles, and other cellular components. Dynein also plays a role in cell motility, such as the movement of cilia and flagella Cell membrane protein (Option B): These proteins are involved in forming channels, receptors, and anchors in the cell membrane, but dynein operates within the cytoplasm, not at the membrane. Cell organelle adherent protein (Option C): Dynein’s primary role is transport rather than adherence. Intracellular junctional protein (Option D): These proteins are involved in cell-cell adhesion and communication (e.g., cadherins, connexins), whereas dynein's function is intracellular transport along the cytoskeleton. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: "caption_element"> {{caption_text}} Definition Inflammation of inner structures of the eye (uveal tissue and retina) with exudates in the vitreous, anterior, and posterior chambers. It spares sclera. Acute bacterial endophthalmitis happens 1-7 days post intraocular surgery M/C causative organism Staphylococcus epidermidis Presentation Severe ocular pain Redness Lacrimation Photophobia Loss of vision Red and swollen lids Conjunctival chemosis Circumcorneal congestion Cloudy cornea Ring infiltration Yellow necrotic wound edges Hypopyon Oedematous and muddy iris Yellow pupil reflex due to purulent exudation Vitreous exudation which causes amaurotic cat's-eye reflex Raised intraocular pressure initially Treatment Intravitreal antibiotics (Option A) : First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Ceftazidime 2.25 mg Second choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Amikacin 0.4 mg Topical antibiotics (Option D) Systemic antibiotics Steroid Therapy Supportive Therapy Vitrectomy - if no improvement in 48-72 hours (Option B) or if severe infection with vision reduced to hand movements close to the face If blind - no perception of light - Evisceration. questions.solutionHtml:
"caption_element">

Definition
  • Inflammation of inner structures of the eye (uveal tissue and retina) with exudates in the vitreous, anterior, and posterior chambers. It spares sclera.
  • Acute bacterial endophthalmitis happens 1-7 days post intraocular surgery

M/C causative organism
  • Staphylococcus epidermidis

Presentation

  • Severe ocular pain
  • Redness
  • Lacrimation
  • Photophobia
  • Loss of vision
  • Red and swollen lids
  • Conjunctival chemosis
  • Circumcorneal congestion
  • Cloudy cornea
  • Ring infiltration
  • Yellow necrotic wound edges
  • Hypopyon
  • Oedematous and muddy iris
  • Yellow pupil reflex due to purulent exudation
  • Vitreous exudation which causes amaurotic cat's-eye reflex
  • Raised intraocular pressure initially

Treatment

  • Intravitreal antibiotics (Option A):
    • First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Ceftazidime 2.25 mg
    • Second choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Amikacin 0.4 mg
  • Topical antibiotics (Option D)
  • Systemic antibiotics
  • Steroid Therapy
  • Supportive Therapy
  • Vitrectomy - if no improvement in 48-72 hours (Option B) or if severe infection with vision reduced to hand movements close to the face
  • If blind - no perception of light - Evisceration.

Redo surgery (Option C) is not the right surgical approach for endophthalmitis.

questions.stem: Patient, who is on antipsychotic medication for his schizophrenia, started to have dystonia. Management of this patient is by?
questions.stemHtml: Patient, who is on antipsychotic medication for his schizophrenia, started to have dystonia. Management of this patient is by?
questions.solution: ul> Anticholinergic medications like benzhexol (which acts on the parasympathetic nervous system by inhibiting efferent pulses directly) can be used to treat Acute Dystonia . It refers to brief, sudden muscle contractions that lead to abnormal movements or postures. This extrapyramidal side effect, commonly seen with antipsychotic medications, occurs when there is a disruption in the nigrostriatal pathway, which plays a key role in motor control. Clinical manifestations: Oculogyric crises (upward rolling of eyes) Tongue protrusion Trismus (jaw muscles) Torticollis (neck muscles twisting to one side) Laryngospasm Dysarthria, Dysphasia (glossopharyngeal symptoms) Dystonic postures of the limbs and trunk. Management: Anticholinergic drugs: Parenteral (IV or IM) is for immediate treatment Oral is used for prophylaxis Drugs include Benztropine, Diphenhydramine, and Promethazine. Replace with fluphenazine (Option B): Fluphenazine is a first-generation antipsychotic primarily used to treat symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. Increase the dose of haloperidol (Option C): Haloperidol is a first-generation antipsychotic (typical antipsychotic) effective for managing psychosis but is known for a higher risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) such as dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. Clozapine (Option D) is a second-generation antipsychotic specifically indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is known for its efficacy in patients who do not respond to other antipsychotic medications. It can lead to a rare adverse effect, such as granulocytosis. @Neet_pg_bot

Phyllodes tumour (Option B) can have similar histological features with ductal proliferation but is typically more cellular and can have a leaf-like architecture. It also tends to grow rapidly and is more common in older women.   3. Bare nuclei - cytoplasm is stripped of,f and only nuclei are visible in blue colour.

Phyllodes tumour (Option B) can have similar histological features with ductal proliferation but is typically more cellular and can have a leaf-like architecture. It also tends to grow rapidly and is more common in older women.

Carcinoma breast (Option D) would be expected to present with more aggressive histological features, such as invasion of surrounding tissue and atypical cells, rather than benign ductal proliferation.

questions.solutionHtml:
strong>Biliary atresia is a serious condition that causes bile ducts to become obstructed or absent, leading to cholestasis and liver damage. In newborns, jaundice that persists beyond 2 weeks is a key clinical sign of biliary atresia, as physiological jaundice typically resolves within the first 1-2 weeks of life.

Extra-Hepatic Biliary Atresia:

  • Also known as Non-Cystic Obliterative Cholangiopathy.
  • Characterised by complete obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts and intrahepatic ducts at the hilum.
  • Typically appear by 2 to 6 weeks of age
    • Jaundice (yellowish coloration of skin and sclera)
    • Abnormally pale stools
    • Dark urine
  • Commonly associated with polysplenia or asplenia

Investigations:

  1. Liver Function Tests:
    • Increased conjugated bilirubin.
    • Markers of cholestasis:
      • 5' nucleotidase
      • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
      • GGT (Gamma-glutamyl transferase):
        • Normal: Up to 40 U/L
        • 4x elevation: Intrahepatic causes
        • 10x elevation: Extrahepatic causes
        • Exception: Low in PFIC type I and II
  2. Ultrasound:
    • High-frequency USG (HUS) for neonatal cholestasis.
    • Fasting USG is the gold standard when biliary atresia is suspected.
    • Characteristic findings:
      • Triangular cord sign (hyperechoic areas indicating fibrous/atretic bile duct)
      • Non-visualized gallbladder/micro gallbladder/gallbladder ghost
  3. Radionucleotide Study:
    • HIDA Scan (Hepatobiliary scan with Tc labelled imino-di-acetic acid):
      • Used as a screening test.
      • Decreased tracer excretion due to obstruction
    • Phenobarbitone loading/priming (5 days) to improve tracer uptake
    • Used as a screening test, not specific
  4. Best Investigation:
    • Liver biopsy: IOC for confirming diagnosis.

Surgical Management:

  •  
  • Temporary procedure: Kasai procedure/hepaticojejunostomy
  • Definitive management: Liver transplantation
  • Kasai Procedure:
    • Temporary procedure
    • Creates communication between the liver and jejunum for bile drainage
    • Should be performed within 8 weeks after birth

questions.solution: f Breast Changes: Mamogenesis: Growth of both ductal and lobuloalveolar system An intact nerve supply is not essential for the growth of mammary glands during pregnancy Lactogenesis: The alveolar cells are the principal sites for the production of milk Milk secretion actually starts on 3rd or 4th postpartum day Galactokinesis: Oxytocin is the major galactokinetic hormone Discharge of milk from the mammary glands depends on suckling and contractile mechanism Galactopoiesis: Prolactin appears to be the single most important galactopoietic hormone For maintenance of effective and continuous lactation, frequency of suckling (>8/24 hours) is essential Options A, B & D are incorrect as they do not follow the physiological sequence of breast changes during pregnancy and lactation. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Mamogenesis:

questions.stem: A patient has muffled heart sounds with low blood pressure. What is the correct JVP finding?
questions.stemHtml: A patient has muffled heart sounds with low blood pressure. What is the correct JVP finding?
questions.solution: n class="customMeta" data-dictid="3ca731b15316927771898437884f89">heart sounds with low blood pressure indicate cardiac tamponade , which is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space, leading to compromised cardiac filling and subsequent hemodynamic compromise. In cardiac tamponade, the characteristic finding is absent y descent and non-pulsatile elevated JVP due to impaired right ventricular filling during diastole. The condition presents with Beck's triad , which includes muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated JVP. Cardiac Tamponade Definition A condition where the cardiac chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow. Fluid accumulation of as little as 200 ml to upwards of 2L may lead to cardiac tamponade development. Clinical Features Beck's triad Jugular Venous Distension : Due to increased central venous pressure. Prominent x descent and an absent y descent. Hypotension : Resulting from impaired cardiac output. Muffled Heart Sounds : Caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial space, dampening heart sounds. Other features Pulsus Paradoxus : A drop in systolic BP during inspiration, greater than 10 mm Hg. Causes of Pulsus paradoxus: Lung Conditions: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism. Heart Conditions: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis. Steep x descent (Option A): Steep x descent is typically seen in constrictive pericarditis. Although prominent x descent is also seen in cardiac tamponade, absent y descent is a more highlighting feature typical of cardiac tamponade. Steep y descent (Option C): Steep y descent is observed in exaggerated tricuspid regurgitation, which allows for rapid right atrial emptying during diastole. Blunted x descent (Option D): Blunted x descent is seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy where there is impaired ventricular relaxation. The clinical presentation of muffled heart sounds and hypotension is more consistent with cardiac tamponade rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy. @Neet_pg_bot

  • In cardiac tamponade, the characteristic finding is absent y descent and non-pulsatile elevated JVP due to impaired right ventricular filling during diastole. The condition presents with Beck's triad, which includes muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated JVP.

    • Cardiac Tamponade

    Definition

    A condition where the cardiac chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow. Fluid accumulation of as little as 200 ml to upwards of 2L may lead to cardiac tamponade development.

    Clinical Features

    Beck's triad

    • Jugular Venous Distension: Due to increased central venous pressure. Prominent x descent and an absent y descent.
    • Hypotension: Resulting from impaired cardiac output.
    • Muffled Heart Sounds: Caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial space, dampening heart sounds.

    Other features

    Pulsus Paradoxus: A drop in systolic BP during inspiration, greater than 10 mm Hg.

    Causes of Pulsus paradoxus:

    • Lung Conditions: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism.
    • Heart Conditions: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis.

     

    Steep x descent (Option A): Steep x descent is typically seen in constrictive pericarditis. Although prominent x descent is also seen in cardiac tamponade, absent y descent is a more highlighting feature typical of cardiac tamponade.

    Steep y descent (Option C): Steep y descent is observed in exaggerated tricuspid regurgitation, which allows for rapid right atrial emptying during diastole.

    Blunted x descent (Option D): Blunted x descent is seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy where there is impaired ventricular relaxation. The clinical presentation of muffled heart sounds and hypotension is more consistent with cardiac tamponade rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway?
questions.solution: s the rate-limiting step of the HMP pathway. It catalyzes the oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH, which is critical for reductive biosynthesis and maintaining cellular redox balance. The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is essential in erythrocytes because it generates NADPH. NADPH is crucial for maintaining glutathione in its reduced form, which is necessary for the activity of glutathione peroxidase. This enzyme removes harmful hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), protecting red blood cells from oxidative damage and preventing hemolysis. Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP) The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP), also known as the hexose monophosphate shunt, is an alternative metabolic pathway for glucose that doesn't generate ATP. Location: Cytosol It serves two primary functions: NADPH Production The PPP is a major source of NADPH, vital for biosynthesis (fatty acids and steroids). NADPH Production: RBCs rely on glycolysis for ATP due to the lack of mitochondria and depend solely on the PPP for NADPH, as they lack mitochondrial dehydrogenases. Glutathione Maintenance: NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, enabling glutathione peroxidase to neutralize hydrogen peroxide and prevent oxidative damage. Impact of NADPH Deficiency : Low NADPH reduces glutathione, impairs glutathione peroxidase, increases oxidative damage , and leads to hemolysis . Ribose-5-Phosphate (R-5-P) Synthesis Ribose-5-phosphate is essential for nucleotide synthesis needed for RNA and DNA. Homeostasis between NADPH and R-5-P production. When NADPH demand exceeds R-5-P's need, the non-oxidative phase converts R-5-P to glycolytic intermediates (fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate). If the demand for R-5-P is higher than for NADPH, the non-oxidative phase generates R-5-P from fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, bypassing the oxidative steps. Differences from Glycolysis Uses NADP+ instead of NAD+ and generates CO2, not ATP. Glucose-6-phosphatase (Option A): This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose during gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. It is not involved in the HMP pathway. Phosphofructokinase-1 (Option C): This enzyme is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis , not the HMP pathway. Glycogen phosphorylase (Option D): This enzyme catalyzes the breakdown of glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate in glycogenolysis and is not related to the HMP pathway. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP)

    The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP), also known as the hexose monophosphate shunt, is an alternative metabolic pathway for glucose that doesn't generate ATP.

    Location: Cytosol
    It serves two primary functions:

    NADPH Production
    • The PPP is a major source of NADPH, vital for biosynthesis (fatty acids and steroids).
    • NADPH Production: RBCs rely on glycolysis for ATP due to the lack of mitochondria and depend solely on the PPP for NADPH, as they lack mitochondrial dehydrogenases.
    • Glutathione Maintenance: NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, enabling glutathione peroxidase to neutralize hydrogen peroxide and prevent oxidative damage.
    • Impact of NADPH Deficiency: Low NADPH reduces glutathione, impairs glutathione peroxidase, increases oxidative damage, and leads to hemolysis.

    Ribose-5-Phosphate (R-5-P) Synthesis
    • Ribose-5-phosphate is essential for nucleotide synthesis needed for RNA and DNA.

    Homeostasis between NADPH and R-5-P

    production.
    • When NADPH demand exceeds R-5-P's need, the non-oxidative phase converts R-5-P to glycolytic intermediates (fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate).
    • If the demand for R-5-P is higher than for NADPH, the non-oxidative phase generates R-5-P from fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, bypassing the oxidative steps.

    Differences from Glycolysis
    • Uses NADP+ instead of NAD+ and generates CO2, not ATP.

    Phosphofructokinase-1 (Option C): This enzyme is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, not the HMP pathway.

ARF is a complication of Group A Streptococcus (GAS) throat infection, often following untreated or inadequately treated strep throat. The main goals in the treatment of ARF are to reduce inflammation , prevent further damage to the heart , and manage symptoms such as joint pain and fever. Management of ARF Treatment for Medication used Group streptococcal infection Penicillin/Erythromycin/Azithromycin. 10 days or oral Amoxicillin or a single dose of IM benzathine penicillin. Azithromycin in case of Penicillin allergy. Symptomatic management Salicylates like aspirin (NSAIDs as an alternative option) It is the first-line treatment for arthritis , fever , and inflammation . Dose: High initially, then taper as symptoms improve. Carditis Corticosteroids. Diuretics like Furosemide are used if heart failure symptoms due to rheumatic carditis are present. (Option D ruled out) Chorea It is managed conservatively, or Valproic acid is used for the sedation CCF Diuretics and vasodilators are used. Prophylaxis (is essential to prevent recurrent infections and further damage to the heart) Inj. Benzathine penicillin is given every 3-4 weeks IM 6 lakh IU in children ≤27 kg. 1.2 million IU in children >27 kg Bed rest is advised Digoxin (Option A) is a cardiac glycoside used to treat conditions like heart failure and atrial fibrillation . It is not used to treat acute rheumatic fever, unless there is heart failure due to rheumatic carditis . Even then, it would only be used as a supportive therapy , not as the primary treatment for ARF. Amiodarone (Option C) is an antiarrhythmic drug mainly used for arrhythmias like ventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation . It may be used in patients with arrhythmias that can occur as a consequence of RHD, but it is not the drug of choice for treating acute rheumatic fever itself. @Neet_pg_bot

    Chorea

    CCF

    Diuretics and vasodilators are used.

    Prophylaxis

    (is essential to prevent recurrent infections and further damage to the heart)

    Inj. Benzathine penicillin is given every 3-4 weeks IM

    • 6 lakh IU in children ≤27 kg.
    • 1.2 million IU in children >27 kg

    Bed rest is advised

    Digoxin (Option A) is a cardiac glycoside used to treat conditions like heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Even then, it would only be used as a supportive therapy, not as the primary treatment for ARF.

questions.solutionHtml:
tomMeta" data-dictid="b913f965781692777194c867946afe">otitis externa

Explanation:

  • It is a pseudomonas infection
  • It is reddish polypoidal lesion at the junction of cartilage and bone which bleeds on touch, seen especially in diabetics and patients with uncontrolled HBA1c

 

Malignant (Necrotizing) Otitis Externa (MOE)

  • Inflammatory condition caused by Pseudomonas infection.
  • Commonly affects elderly diabetic patients or those on immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Severe ear pain, granulations in the ear canal, and facial paralysis are common symptoms.
  • Infection can spread to the skull base, jugular foramen, and cause multiple cranial nerve palsies.

Etiopathogenesis:

  • Early presentation mimics diffuse otitis externa but with intense pain.
  • Granulations in the ear canal indicate disease progression.
  • Infection can extend:
    • Anteriorly to the temporomandibular fossa.
    • Posteriorly to the mastoid.
    • Medially into the middle ear and petrous bone.

Investigations:

  • Clinical suspicion based on severe otalgia and granulation tissue in elderly diabetics.
  • Imaging:
    • CT scan/MRI: Shows bone destruction and soft tissue involvement.
    • Gallium-67 scan: Indicates soft tissue infection; useful for diagnosis and follow-up.
    • Technetium-99 bone scan: Detects bone infection but not useful for disease monitoring due to prolonged positivity.

Treatment:

  • Control of diabetes: Essential for management.
  • Ear canal toilet: Clean the ear, remove discharge, debris, and granulations.
  • Antibiotics:
    • IV Gentamicin with Ticarcillin (both ototoxic/nephrotoxic).
    • Third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone or Ceftazidime), combined with an aminoglycoside.
    • Quinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally) can be combined with Rifampin.
    • Antibiotic therapy typically lasts 6-8 weeks or longer.
  • Culture and sensitivity of ear discharge to adjust antibiotics if non-responsive to treatment.
  • Prolonged antibiotic treatment has largely replaced the need for radical surgery.

 

Incorrect Options:

Otitis externa (Option A):

  • It is characterized by pain during jaw movement and can be seen in diabetics but not associated with any blood stained- ear discharge

 

Serous otitis media (Option C):

  • Excrutuiation pain and blood stained ear discharge are not features of serous otitis media

 

Otomycosis (Option D):

  • It is caused by Aspergillus niger/ Candida species in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressant persons and most often in immunocompromised people.
  • It is characterized by white-ish discharge with black spores (Wet newspaper-like appearance) and the main symptom as itching in the external auditory canal.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man came for a follow-up after recently receiving a new diagnosis and treatment initiation. He is counseled about the Axshya project. Which of the following diseases was this patient diagnosed with?
questions.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man came for a follow-up after recently receiving a new diagnosis and treatment initiation. He is counseled about the Axshya project. Which of the following diseases was this patient diagnosed with?
questions.solution: Correct Option: A) Tuberculosis Project Axshya is a collaborative initiative aimed at improving TB control efforts in India. It focuses on strengthening TB care and control services, including early detection, diagnosis, and treatment of TB cases. The project includes strategies such as community mobilization, awareness campaigns, and active case finding to reach vulnerable populations and reduce the TB burden. Incorrect Options: Options B, C, and D: Project Axshya does not deal with any of these diseases. @Neet_pg_bot
